# jsonptr 0.7.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/jsonptr/0.7.1

# jsonptr - JSON Pointers (RFC 6901) for Rust

JSON Pointers ([RFC 6901](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6901))
defines a string syntax for identifying a specific location within a JSON, or
similar, document. This crate provides two types, [ Pointer](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/struct.Pointer.html) and

[(akin to](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/struct.PointerBuf.html)

`PointerBuf`[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.Path.html)

`Path`[), for working with them abstractly.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.PathBuf.html)

`PathBuf`A pointer is composed of zero or more [ Token](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/struct.Token.html)s, single segments which
represent a field of an object or an

[of an array, and are bounded by either](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/index/index.html)

`index``'/'` or the end of the string. Tokens are lightly encoded, where `'~'`
is escaped as `"~0"` due to it signaling encoding and `'/'` is escaped as `"~1"`
because `'/'` separates tokens and would split the token into two otherwise.[ Token](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/struct.Token.html)s can be iterated over using either

[, returned from the](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/struct.Tokens.html)

`Tokens`[method of a pointer or](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/struct.Tokens.html)

`tokens`[, returned from the](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/struct.Components.html)

`Components`[method. The difference being that](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/struct.Components.html)

`components``Tokens` iterates over each
token in the pointer, while `Components` iterates over [s, which can represent the root of the document or a single token of the pointer.](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/enum.Component.html)

`Component`Operations [ resolve](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/resolve/index.html),

[and](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/assign/index.html)

`assign`[are provided as traits with corresponding methods on pointer types. Implementations of each trait are provided for value types of the crates](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/delete/index.html)

`delete`[and](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1.0/serde_json/enum.Value.html)

`serde_json`[. All operations are enabled by default but are gated by](https://docs.rs/toml/0.8/toml/enum.Value.html)

`toml`[feature flags](https://docs.rs#feature-flags).

## Usage

### Parsing and General Usage

To parse a [ Pointer](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/struct.Pointer.html) from a string, use either

[, for potentially fallible parsing, or the](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/struct.Pointer.html#method.parse)

`Pointer::parse``const fn` `from_static` to produce a
`&'static Pointer` from a string that is known to be valid.```
use Pointer;
let ptr = parse.unwrap;
let static_ptr = from_static;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
let parent = ptr.parent.unwrap;
assert_eq!;
let  = ptr.split_front.unwrap;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
[ PointerBuf](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/struct.PointerBuf.html)s can be parsed using

[or constructed from an iterator of](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/struct.PointerBuf.html#method.parse)

`PointerBuf::parse`[s with the](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/struct.Token.html)

`Token`[method:](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/struct.PointerBuf.html#method.from_tokens)

`from_tokens````
use PointerBuf;
let mut buf = parse.unwrap;
let from_tokens = from_tokens;
assert_eq!;
buf.push_front;
buf.push_front;
buf.push_back;
assert_eq!;
```
### Token Iteration

Iterating over the tokens or components of a pointer:

```
use ;
let ptr = from_static;
//  Using the `tokens` method:
let tokens:  = ptr.tokens.collect;
assert_eq!;
// Using the `components` method:
let mut components = ptr.components;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
### Resolving Values

To get a value at the location of a pointer, use either the [ Resolve](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/resolve/index.html) and

[traits or](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/resolve/trait.ResolveMut.html)

`ResolveMut`[and](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/struct.Pointer.html#method.resolve)

`Pointer::resolve`[methods. See the](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/struct.Pointer.html#method.resolve_mut)

`Pointer::resolve_mut`[mod for more information.](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/resolve/index.html)

`resolve````
use Pointer;
use json;
let ptr = parse.unwrap;
let data = json!;
let bar = ptr.resolve.unwrap;
assert_eq!;
```
### Assigning Values

Values can be set, with path expansion, using the either the [ Assign](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/assign/index.html) trait or

[. See](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/struct.Pointer.html#method.assign)

`Pointer::assign`[for more information.](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/assign/index.html)

`assign````
use Pointer;
use json;
let ptr = parse.unwrap;
let mut data = json!;
let replaced = ptr.assign.unwrap;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
### Deleting Values

Values can be removed with the either the [ Delete](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/delete/index.html) trait or

[. See](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/struct.Pointer.html#method.delete)

`Pointer::delete`[for more information.](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/delete/index.html)

`delete````
use Pointer;
use json;
let ptr = parse.unwrap;
let mut data = json!;
let replaced = ptr.assign.unwrap;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
### Error Reporting

Any error produced by function calls into methods of traits or types of this
crate can be converted into a [`Report`] which contains the original error
and the [`String`] which failed to parse or the [ PointerBuf](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/struct.PointerBuf.html) which failed to
resolve or assign.

```
    use ;
    let ptr_str = "foo/bar";
    let err /* Result<&Pointer, Report<ParseError>> */ = parse.diagnose.unwrap_err;
    assert!;
```
In the case of [ PointerBuf::parse](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/struct.PointerBuf.html#method.parse), the [

`ParseError`] is always wrapped in a
[`Report`] so that the input `String` is not dropped.```
    use ;
    let ptr_str = "foo/bar";
    let err /* Result<&PointerBuf, Report<ParseError>> */ = parse.unwrap_err;
    assert!;
```
## Feature Flags

| Flag | Description | Enables | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"std"` | Implements `std::error::Error`for error types | ✓ | |
| `"serde"` | Enables support for types`serde` | ✓ | |

| `"delete"` | Enables the module and related pointer methods, providing a means to delete a value at a specific location within a document`delete` | `"resolve"` | ✓ |
| `"miette"` | Enables integration with for error reporting`miette` | `"std"` |

# jsonptr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/jsonptr/0.7.1/target-redirect/jsonptr/

## Expand description

JSON Pointers ([RFC 6901](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6901))
defines a string syntax for identifying a specific location within a JSON, or
similar, document. This crate provides two types, [ Pointer](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/struct.Pointer.html) and

[(akin to](https://docs.rs/struct.PointerBuf.html)

`PointerBuf`[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.Path.html)

`Path`[), for working with them abstractly.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.PathBuf.html)

`PathBuf`A pointer is composed of zero or more [ Token](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html)s, single segments which
represent a field of an object or an

[of an array, and are bounded by either](https://docs.rs/index/index.html)

`index``'/'` or the end of the string. Tokens are lightly encoded, where `'~'`
is escaped as `"~0"` due to it signaling encoding and `'/'` is escaped as `"~1"`
because `'/'` separates tokens and would split the token into two otherwise.[ Token](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html)s can be iterated over using either

[, returned from the](https://docs.rs/struct.Tokens.html)

`Tokens`[method of a pointer or](https://docs.rs/struct.Tokens.html)

`tokens`[, returned from the](https://docs.rs/struct.Components.html)

`Components`[method. The difference being that](https://docs.rs/struct.Components.html)

`components``Tokens` iterates over each
token in the pointer, while `Components` iterates over [s, which can represent the root of the document or a single token of the pointer.](https://docs.rs/enum.Component.html)

`Component`Operations [ resolve](https://docs.rs/resolve/index.html),

[and](crate::asign)

`assign`[are provided as traits with corresponding methods on pointer types. Implementations of each trait are provided for value types of the crates](https://docs.rs/delete/index.html)

`delete`[and](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1.0/serde_json/enum.Value.html)

`serde_json`[. All operations are enabled by default but are gated by](https://docs.rs/toml/0.8/toml/enum.Value.html)

`toml`[feature flags](https://docs.rs#feature-flags).

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-and-general-usage)Parsing and General Usage

To parse a [ Pointer](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/struct.Pointer.html) from a string, use either

[, for potentially fallible parsing, or the](https://docs.rs/struct.Pointer.html#method.parse)

`Pointer::parse``const fn` `from_static` to produce a
`&'static Pointer` from a string that is known to be valid.```
use jsonptr::Pointer;
let ptr = Pointer::parse("/examples/0/name").unwrap();
let static_ptr = Pointer::from_static("/examples/0/name");
assert_eq!(ptr, static_ptr);
assert_eq!(ptr.get(1..).unwrap(), Pointer::parse("/0/name").unwrap());
let parent = ptr.parent().unwrap();
assert_eq!(parent, Pointer::parse("/examples/0").unwrap());
let (token, remaining) = ptr.split_front().unwrap();
assert_eq!(token.decoded(), "examples");
assert_eq!(remaining, Pointer::parse("/0/name").unwrap());
```
[ PointerBuf](https://docs.rs/struct.PointerBuf.html)s can be parsed using

[or constructed from an iterator of](https://docs.rs/struct.PointerBuf.html#method.parse)

`PointerBuf::parse`[s with the](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html)

`Token`[method:](https://docs.rs/struct.PointerBuf.html#method.from_tokens)

`from_tokens````
use jsonptr::PointerBuf;
let mut buf = PointerBuf::parse("/examples/0/name").unwrap();
let from_tokens = PointerBuf::from_tokens(["examples", "0", "name"]);
assert_eq!(&buf, &from_tokens);
buf.push_front("pointer");
buf.push_front("~");
buf.push_back("/");
assert_eq!(buf.as_str(), "/~0/pointer/examples/0/name/~1");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#token-iteration)Token Iteration

Iterating over the tokens or components of a pointer:

```
use jsonptr::{Pointer, Component, Token};
let ptr = Pointer::from_static("/path/to/value");
//  Using the `tokens` method:
let tokens: Vec<_> = ptr.tokens().collect();
assert_eq!(tokens, vec![Token::new("path"), Token::new("to"), Token::new("value")]);
// Using the `components` method:
let mut components = ptr.components();
assert_eq!(components.next(), Some(Component::Root));
assert_eq!(components.next(), Some(Component::Token(Token::new("path"))));
assert_eq!(components.next(), Some(Component::Token(Token::new("to"))));
assert_eq!(components.next(), Some(Component::Token(Token::new("value"))));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#resolving-values)Resolving Values

To get a value at the location of a pointer, use either the [ Resolve](https://docs.rs/resolve/index.html) and

[traits or](https://docs.rs/resolve/trait.ResolveMut.html)

`ResolveMut`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Pointer.html#method.resolve)

`Pointer::resolve`[methods. See the](https://docs.rs/struct.Pointer.html#method.resolve_mut)

`Pointer::resolve_mut`[mod for more information.](https://docs.rs/resolve/index.html)

`resolve````
use jsonptr::Pointer;
use serde_json::json;
let ptr = Pointer::parse("/foo/bar").unwrap();
let data = json!({"foo": { "bar": 34 }});
let bar = ptr.resolve(&data).unwrap();
assert_eq!(bar, &json!(34));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#assigning-values)Assigning Values

Values can be set, with path expansion, using the either the [ Assign](crate::asign) trait or

[. See](https://docs.rs/struct.Pointer.html#method.assign)

`Pointer::assign`[for more information.](crate::asign)

`assign````
use jsonptr::Pointer;
use serde_json::json;
let ptr = Pointer::parse("/secret/universe").unwrap();
let mut data = json!({"secret": { "universe": 42 }});
let replaced = ptr.assign(&mut data, json!(34)).unwrap();
assert_eq!(replaced, Some(json!(42)));
assert_eq!(data, json!({"secret": { "universe": 34 }}));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#deleting-values)Deleting Values

Values can be removed with the either the [ Delete](https://docs.rs/delete/index.html) trait or

[. See](https://docs.rs/struct.Pointer.html#method.delete)

`Pointer::delete`[for more information.](https://docs.rs/delete/index.html)

`delete````
use jsonptr::Pointer;
use serde_json::json;

assert_eq!(data, json!({"secret": { "universe": 34 }}));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#error-reporting)Error Reporting

Any error produced by function calls into methods of traits or types of this
crate can be converted into a [ Report](https://docs.rs/diagnostic/struct.Report.html) which contains the original error
and the

[which failed to parse or the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

`String`[which failed to resolve or assign.](https://docs.rs/struct.PointerBuf.html)

`PointerBuf````
    use jsonptr::{Pointer, Diagnose};
    let ptr_str = "foo/bar";
    let err /* Result<&Pointer, Report<ParseError>> */ = Pointer::parse(ptr_str).diagnose(ptr_str).unwrap_err();
    assert!(err.original().is_no_leading_slash());
```
In the case of [ PointerBuf::parse](https://docs.rs/struct.PointerBuf.html#method.parse), the

[is always wrapped in a](https://docs.rs/enum.ParseError.html)

`ParseError`[so that the input](https://docs.rs/diagnostic/struct.Report.html)

`Report``String` is not dropped.```
    use jsonptr::{PointerBuf};
    let ptr_str = "foo/bar";
    let err /* Result<&PointerBuf, Report<ParseError>> */ = PointerBuf::parse(ptr_str).unwrap_err();
    assert!(err.original().is_no_leading_slash());
```

# jsonptr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/jsonptr/0.7.1/jsonptr/index.html

## Expand description

JSON Pointers ([RFC 6901](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6901))
defines a string syntax for identifying a specific location within a JSON, or
similar, document. This crate provides two types, [ Pointer](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/struct.Pointer.html) and

[(akin to](https://docs.rs/struct.PointerBuf.html)

`PointerBuf`[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.Path.html)

`Path`[), for working with them abstractly.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.PathBuf.html)

`PathBuf`A pointer is composed of zero or more [ Token](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html)s, single segments which
represent a field of an object or an

[of an array, and are bounded by either](https://docs.rs/index/index.html)

`index``'/'` or the end of the string. Tokens are lightly encoded, where `'~'`
is escaped as `"~0"` due to it signaling encoding and `'/'` is escaped as `"~1"`
because `'/'` separates tokens and would split the token into two otherwise.[ Token](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html)s can be iterated over using either

[, returned from the](https://docs.rs/struct.Tokens.html)

`Tokens`[method of a pointer or](https://docs.rs/struct.Tokens.html)

`tokens`[, returned from the](https://docs.rs/struct.Components.html)

`Components`[method. The difference being that](https://docs.rs/struct.Components.html)

`components``Tokens` iterates over each
token in the pointer, while `Components` iterates over [s, which can represent the root of the document or a single token of the pointer.](https://docs.rs/enum.Component.html)

`Component`Operations [ resolve](https://docs.rs/resolve/index.html),

[and](crate::asign)

`assign`[are provided as traits with corresponding methods on pointer types. Implementations of each trait are provided for value types of the crates](https://docs.rs/delete/index.html)

`delete`[and](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1.0/serde_json/enum.Value.html)

`serde_json`[. All operations are enabled by default but are gated by](https://docs.rs/toml/0.8/toml/enum.Value.html)

`toml`[feature flags](https://docs.rs#feature-flags).

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-and-general-usage)Parsing and General Usage

To parse a [ Pointer](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/struct.Pointer.html) from a string, use either

[, for potentially fallible parsing, or the](https://docs.rs/struct.Pointer.html#method.parse)

`Pointer::parse``const fn` `from_static` to produce a
`&'static Pointer` from a string that is known to be valid.```
use jsonptr::Pointer;
let ptr = Pointer::parse("/examples/0/name").unwrap();
let static_ptr = Pointer::from_static("/examples/0/name");
assert_eq!(ptr, static_ptr);
assert_eq!(ptr.get(1..).unwrap(), Pointer::parse("/0/name").unwrap());
let parent = ptr.parent().unwrap();
assert_eq!(parent, Pointer::parse("/examples/0").unwrap());
let (token, remaining) = ptr.split_front().unwrap();
assert_eq!(token.decoded(), "examples");
assert_eq!(remaining, Pointer::parse("/0/name").unwrap());
```
[ PointerBuf](https://docs.rs/struct.PointerBuf.html)s can be parsed using

[or constructed from an iterator of](https://docs.rs/struct.PointerBuf.html#method.parse)

`PointerBuf::parse`[s with the](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html)

`Token`[method:](https://docs.rs/struct.PointerBuf.html#method.from_tokens)

`from_tokens````
use jsonptr::PointerBuf;
let mut buf = PointerBuf::parse("/examples/0/name").unwrap();
let from_tokens = PointerBuf::from_tokens(["examples", "0", "name"]);
assert_eq!(&buf, &from_tokens);
buf.push_front("pointer");
buf.push_front("~");
buf.push_back("/");
assert_eq!(buf.as_str(), "/~0/pointer/examples/0/name/~1");
```

# PointerBuf in jsonptr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/jsonptr/0.7.1/jsonptr/struct.PointerBuf.html

`pub struct PointerBuf(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

An owned, mutable [ Pointer](https://docs.rs/struct.Pointer.html) (akin to

`String`).This type provides methods like [ PointerBuf::push_back](https://docs.rs/struct.PointerBuf.html#method.push_back) and

[that mutate the pointer in place. It also implements](https://docs.rs/struct.PointerBuf.html#method.replace)

`PointerBuf::replace`[to](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/deref/trait.Deref.html)

`core::ops::Deref`[, meaning that all methods on](https://docs.rs/struct.Pointer.html)

`Pointer`[slices are available on](https://docs.rs/struct.Pointer.html)

`Pointer``PointerBuf` values as well.## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jsonptr/pointer.rs.html#181-207)#### pub fn [split_front](https://docs.rs#method.split_front)(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<([Token](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html)<'_>, &Self)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jsonptr/pointer.rs.html#181-207)

#### pub fn [split_front](https://docs.rs#method.split_front)(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<([Token](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html)<'_>, &Self)>

Splits the `Pointer` into the first `Token` and a remainder `Pointer`.

Splits the `Pointer` at the given index if the character at the index is
a separator slash (`'/'`), returning `Some((head, tail))`. Otherwise,
returns `None`.

For the following JSON Pointer, the following splits are possible (0, 4, 8):

```
/foo/bar/baz
↑   ↑   ↑
0   4   8
```
All other indices will return `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
let ptr = Pointer::from_static("/foo/bar/baz");
let (head, tail) = ptr.split_at(4).unwrap();
assert_eq!(head, Pointer::from_static("/foo"));
assert_eq!(tail, Pointer::from_static("/bar/baz"));
assert_eq!(ptr.split_at(3), None);
```

itself).

Attempts to get a `Token` by the index. Returns `None` if the index is
out of bounds.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
use jsonptr::{Pointer, Token};
let ptr = Pointer::from_static("/foo/bar/qux");
assert_eq!(ptr.get(0), Some("foo".into()));
assert_eq!(ptr.get(1), Some("bar".into()));
assert_eq!(ptr.get(3), None);
assert_eq!(ptr.get(..), Some(Pointer::from_static("/foo/bar/qux")));
assert_eq!(ptr.get(..1), Some(Pointer::from_static("/foo")));
assert_eq!(ptr.get(1..3), Some(Pointer::from_static("/bar/qux")));
assert_eq!(ptr.get(1..=2), Some(Pointer::from_static("/bar/qux")));
let ptr = Pointer::root();
assert_eq!(ptr.get(0), None);
assert_eq!(ptr.get(..), Some(Pointer::root()));
```

`ResolveError`[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jsonptr/pointer.rs.html#381-393)#### pub fn [intersection](https://docs.rs#method.intersection)<'a>(&'a self, other: &Self) -> &'a Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jsonptr/pointer.rs.html#381-393)

#### pub fn [intersection](https://docs.rs#method.intersection)<'a>(&'a self, other: &Self) -> &'a Self

Finds the commonality between this and another `Pointer`.

Attempts to delete a `serde_json::Value` based upon the path in this
`Pointer`.

The rules of deletion are determined by the `D`’s implementation of
[ Delete](https://docs.rs/delete/trait.Delete.html). The supplied implementations (

`"json"` & `"toml"`) operate
as follows:- If the `Pointer`can be resolved, the`Value`is deleted and returned.
- If the `Pointer`fails to resolve for any reason,`Ok(None)`is returned.
- If the `Pointer`is root,`value`is replaced:- `"json"`:- `serde_json::Value::Null`
- `"toml"`:- `toml::Value::Table::Default`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#deleting-a-resolved-pointer)Deleting a resolved pointer:

```
use jsonptr::{Pointer, delete::Delete};
use serde_json::json;
let mut data = json!({ "foo": { "bar": { "baz": "qux" } } });
let ptr = Pointer::from_static("/foo/bar/baz");
assert_eq!(data.delete(&ptr), Some("qux".into()));
assert_eq!(data, json!({ "foo": { "bar": {} } }));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#deleting-a-non-existent-pointer-returns-none)Deleting a non-existent Pointer returns `None`:

```
use jsonptr::{ Pointer, delete::Delete };
use serde_json::json;
let mut data = json!({});
let ptr = Pointer::from_static("/foo/bar/baz");
assert_eq!(ptr.delete(&mut data), None);
assert_eq!(data, json!({}));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#deleting-a-root-pointer-replaces-the-value-with-valuenull)Deleting a root pointer replaces the value with `Value::Null`:

```
use jsonptr::{Pointer, delete::Delete};
use serde_json::json;
let mut data = json!({ "foo": { "bar": "baz" } });
let ptr = Pointer::root();
assert_eq!(data.delete(&ptr), Some(json!({ "foo": { "bar": "baz" } })));
assert!(data.is_null());
```
Attempts to assign `src` to `dest` based on the path in this `Pointer`.

If the path is partially available, the missing portions will be created. If the path
contains a zero index, such as `"/0"`, then an array will be created. Otherwise, objects
will be utilized to create the missing path.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-2)Example

```
use jsonptr::Pointer;
use serde_json::{json, Value};
let mut data = json!([]);
let mut ptr = Pointer::from_static("/0/foo");
let replaced = ptr.assign(&mut data, json!("bar")).unwrap();
assert_eq!(data, json!([{"foo": "bar"}]));
assert_eq!(replaced, None);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#errors-4)Errors

Returns [ Assign::Error](https://docs.rs/assign/trait.Assign.html#associatedtype.Error) if the path is invalid or if the value cannot be assigned.

This length expresses the byte count of the underlying string that
represents the RFC 6091 Pointer. See also [`std::str::len`].

```

# Token in jsonptr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/jsonptr/0.7.1/jsonptr/struct.Token.html

`pub struct Token<'a> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A `Token` is a segment of a JSON [ Pointer](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html), preceded by

`'/'` (`%x2F`).`Token`s can represent a key in a JSON object or an index in an array.

- Indexes should not contain leading zeros.
- When dealing with arrays or path expansion for assignment, `"-"`represent the next, non-existent index in a JSON array.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jsonptr/token.rs.html#73-106)#### pub fn [from_encoded](https://docs.rs#method.from_encoded)(s: &'a [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self, [EncodingError](https://docs.rs/struct.EncodingError.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jsonptr/token.rs.html#73-106)

#### pub fn [from_encoded](https://docs.rs#method.from_encoded)(s: &'a [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self, [EncodingError](https://docs.rs/struct.EncodingError.html)>

Constructs a `Token` from an RFC 6901 encoded string.

To be valid, the string must not contain any `/` characters, and any `~`
characters must be followed by either `0` or `1`.

This function does not allocate.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
assert_eq!(Token::from_encoded("~1foo~1~0bar").unwrap().decoded(), "/foo/~bar");
let err = Token::from_encoded("foo/oops~bar").unwrap_err();
assert_eq!(err.offset, 3);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

Returns `InvalidEncodingError` if the input string is not a valid RFC
6901 (`~` must be followed by `0` or `1`)

Constructs a `Token` from an arbitrary string.

If the string contains a `/` or a `~`, then it will be assumed not
encoded, in which case this function will encode it, allocating a new
string.

If the string is already encoded per RFC 6901, use
[ Self::from_encoded](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html#method.from_encoded) instead, otherwise it will end up double-encoded.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

`assert_eq!(Token::new("/foo/~bar").encoded(), "~1foo~1~0bar");`[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jsonptr/token.rs.html#164-168)#### pub fn [into_owned](https://docs.rs#method.into_owned)(self) -> [Token](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html)<'static>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jsonptr/token.rs.html#164-168)

#### pub fn [into_owned](https://docs.rs#method.into_owned)(self) -> [Token](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html)<'static>

Converts into an owned copy of this token.

If the token is not already owned, this will clone the referenced string slice.

Extracts an owned copy of this token.

If the token is not already owned, this will clone the referenced string slice.

This method is like [ Self::into_owned](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html#method.into_owned), except it doesn’t take
ownership of the original

`Token`.[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jsonptr/token.rs.html#262-264)#### pub fn [to_index](https://docs.rs#method.to_index)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Index](https://docs.rs/index/enum.Index.html), [ParseIndexError](https://docs.rs/index/enum.ParseIndexError.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jsonptr/token.rs.html#262-264)

#### pub fn [to_index](https://docs.rs#method.to_index)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Index](https://docs.rs/index/enum.Index.html), [ParseIndexError](https://docs.rs/index/enum.ParseIndexError.html)>

Attempts to parse the given `Token` as an array index.

Per [RFC 6901](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6901#section-4),
the acceptable values are non-negative integers and the `-` character,
which stands for the next, non-existent member after the last array
element.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-4)Examples

```
assert_eq!(Token::new("-").to_index(), Ok(Index::Next));
assert_eq!(Token::new("0").to_index(), Ok(Index::Num(0)));
assert_eq!(Token::new("2").to_index(), Ok(Index::Num(2)));
assert!(Token::new("a").to_index().is_err());
assert!(Token::new("-1").to_index().is_err());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#errors-1)Errors

Returns [ ParseIndexError](https://docs.rs/index/enum.ParseIndexError.html) if the token is not a valid array index.

# jsonptr::delete - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/jsonptr/0.7.1/jsonptr/delete/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#delete-values-based-on-json-pointers)Delete values based on JSON Pointers

This module provides the [ Delete](https://docs.rs/trait.Delete.html) trait which is implemented by types that
can internally remove a value based on a JSON Pointer.

The rules of deletion are determined by the implementation, with the
provided implementations (`"json"` & `"toml"`) operating as follows:

- If the `Pointer``Value``Some(value)`.
- If the `Pointer``Ok(None)`is returned.
- If the `Pointer``value`is replaced:- `"json"`-- `serde_json::Value::Null`
- `"toml"`-- `toml::Value::Table::Default`

This module is enabled by default with the `"delete"` feature flag.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Deleting a resolved pointer:

```
use jsonptr::{Pointer, delete::Delete};
use serde_json::json;
let mut data = json!({ "foo": { "bar": { "baz": "qux" } } });
let ptr = Pointer::from_static("/foo/bar/baz");
assert_eq!(data.delete(&ptr), Some("qux".into()));
assert_eq!(data, json!({ "foo": { "bar": {} } }));
```
Deleting a non-existent Pointer returns `None`:

```
use jsonptr::{ Pointer, delete::Delete };
use serde_json::json;
let mut data = json!({});
let ptr = Pointer::from_static("/foo/bar/baz");
assert_eq!(ptr.delete(&mut data), None);
assert_eq!(data, json!({}));
```
Deleting a root pointer replaces the value with `Value::Null`:

```
use jsonptr::{Pointer, delete::Delete};
use serde_json::json;
let mut data = json!({ "foo": { "bar": "baz" } });
let ptr = Pointer::root();
assert_eq!(data.delete(&ptr), Some(json!({ "foo": { "bar": "baz" } })));
assert!(data.is_null());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#provided-implementations)Provided implementations

| Lang | value type | feature flag | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| JSON | `serde_json::Value` | `"json"` | ✓ |
| TOML | `toml::Value` | `"toml"` |

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Delete](https://docs.rs/trait.Delete.html)
- Delete is implemented by types which can internally remove a value based on a JSON Pointer

# Assign in jsonptr::assign - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/jsonptr/0.7.1/jsonptr/assign/trait.Assign.html

```
pub trait Assign {
    type
```
[Value](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Value);
    type [Error](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Error);
    // Required method
    fn [assign](https://docs.rs#tymethod.assign)<V>(
        &mut self,
        ptr: &[Pointer](https://docs.rs/struct.Pointer.html),
        value: V,
    ) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<Self::[Value](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html#associatedtype.Value)>, Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html#associatedtype.Error)>
       where V: [Into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)<Self::[Value](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html#associatedtype.Value)>;
}## Expand description

Implemented by types which can internally assign a
([ Value](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html#associatedtype.Value)) at a path represented by a JSON

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Pointer.html)

`Pointer`[§](https://docs.rs#expansion)Expansion

For provided implementations (`"json"`, and `"toml"`) path will
automatically be expanded the if the [ Pointer](https://docs.rs/struct.Pointer.html) is not fully exhausted
before reaching a non-existent key in the case of objects, index in the case
of arrays, or a scalar value (including

`null`) based upon a best-guess
effort on the meaning of each [:](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html)

`Token`- If the `Token``"0"`or`"-"`, the token will be considered an index of an array.
- All tokens not equal to `"0"`or`"-"`will be considered keys of an object.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#successful-assignment-with-replacement)Successful assignment with replacement

This example demonstrates a successful assignment with replacement.

```
use jsonptr::{Pointer, assign::Assign};
use serde_json::{json, Value};
let mut data = json!({"foo": "bar"});
let ptr = Pointer::from_static("/foo");
let replaced = data.assign(&ptr, "baz").unwrap();
assert_eq!(replaced, Some(json!("bar")));
assert_eq!(data, json!({"foo": "baz"}));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#successful-assignment-with-path-expansion)Successful assignment with path expansion

This example demonstrates path expansion, including an array index (`"0"`)

```
let ptr = Pointer::from_static("/foo/bar/0/baz");
let mut data = serde_json::json!({"foo": "bar"});
let replaced = data.assign(ptr, json!("qux")).unwrap();
assert_eq!(&data, &json!({"foo": {"bar": [{"baz": "qux"}]}}));
assert_eq!(replaced, Some(json!("bar")));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#successful-assignment-with---token)Successful assignment with `"-"` token

This example performs path expansion using the special `"-"` token (per RFC
6901) to represent the next element in an array.

```
let ptr = Pointer::from_static("/foo/bar/-/baz");
let mut data = json!({"foo": "bar"});
let replaced = data.assign(ptr, json!("qux")).unwrap();
assert_eq!(&data, &json!({"foo": {"bar": [{"baz": "qux"}]}}));
assert_eq!(replaced, Some(json!("bar")));
```

# jsonptr::assign - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/jsonptr/0.7.1/jsonptr/assign/index.html

## Expand description

This module provides the [ Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html) trait which allows for the assignment of
values based on a JSON Pointer.

This module is enabled by default with the `"assign"` feature flag.

[§](https://docs.rs#expansion)Expansion

The path will automatically be expanded if the [ Pointer](https://docs.rs/struct.Pointer.html) is not fully
exhausted before reaching a non-existent key in the case of objects, index
in the case of arrays, or a scalar value (including

`null`) based upon a
best-guess effort on the meaning of each [:](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html)

`Token`- If the `Token``"0"`or`"-"`, the token will be considered an index of an array.
- All tokens not equal to `"0"`or`"-"`will be considered keys of an object.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

[ Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html) can be used directly or through the

[method of](https://docs.rs/struct.Pointer.html#method.assign)

`assign`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Pointer.html)

`Pointer````
use jsonptr::Pointer;
use serde_json::json;
let mut data = json!({"foo": "bar"});
let ptr = Pointer::from_static("/foo");
let replaced = ptr.assign(&mut data, "baz").unwrap();
assert_eq!(replaced, Some(json!("bar")));
assert_eq!(data, json!({"foo": "baz"}));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#provided-implementations)Provided implementations

| Lang | value type | feature flag | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| JSON | `serde_json::Value` | `"json"` | ✓ |
| TOML | `toml::Value` | `"toml"` |

# jsonptr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/

## Expand description

JSON Pointers ([RFC 6901](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6901))
defines a string syntax for identifying a specific location within a JSON, or
similar, document. This crate provides two types, [ Pointer](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/struct.Pointer.html) and

[(akin to](https://docs.rs/struct.PointerBuf.html)

`PointerBuf`[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.Path.html)

`Path`[), for working with them abstractly.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.PathBuf.html)

`PathBuf`A pointer is composed of zero or more [ Token](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html)s, single segments which
represent a field of an object or an

[of an array, and are bounded by either](https://docs.rs/index/index.html)

`index``'/'` or the end of the string. Tokens are lightly encoded, where `'~'`
is escaped as `"~0"` due to it signaling encoding and `'/'` is escaped as `"~1"`
because `'/'` separates tokens and would split the token into two otherwise.[ Token](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html)s can be iterated over using either

[, returned from the](https://docs.rs/struct.Tokens.html)

`Tokens`[method of a pointer or](https://docs.rs/struct.Tokens.html)

`tokens`[, returned from the](https://docs.rs/struct.Components.html)

`Components`[method. The difference being that](https://docs.rs/struct.Components.html)

`components``Tokens` iterates over each
token in the pointer, while `Components` iterates over [s, which can represent the root of the document or a single token of the pointer.](https://docs.rs/enum.Component.html)

`Component`Operations [ resolve](https://docs.rs/resolve/index.html),

[and](crate::asign)

`assign`[are provided as traits with corresponding methods on pointer types. Implementations of each trait are provided for value types of the crates](https://docs.rs/delete/index.html)

`delete`[and](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1.0/serde_json/enum.Value.html)

`serde_json`[. All operations are enabled by default but are gated by](https://docs.rs/toml/0.8/toml/enum.Value.html)

`toml`[feature flags](https://docs.rs#feature-flags).

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-and-general-usage)Parsing and General Usage

To parse a [ Pointer](https://docs.rs/jsonptr/latest/jsonptr/struct.Pointer.html) from a string, use either

[, for potentially fallible parsing, or the](https://docs.rs/struct.Pointer.html#method.parse)

`Pointer::parse``const fn` `from_static` to produce a
`&'static Pointer` from a string that is known to be valid.```
use jsonptr::Pointer;
let ptr = Pointer::parse("/examples/0/name").unwrap();
let static_ptr = Pointer::from_static("/examples/0/name");
assert_eq!(ptr, static_ptr);
assert_eq!(ptr.get(1..).unwrap(), Pointer::parse("/0/name").unwrap());
let parent = ptr.parent().unwrap();
assert_eq!(parent, Pointer::parse("/examples/0").unwrap());
let (token, remaining) = ptr.split_front().unwrap();
assert_eq!(token.decoded(), "examples");
assert_eq!(remaining, Pointer::parse("/0/name").unwrap());
```
[ PointerBuf](https://docs.rs/struct.PointerBuf.html)s can be parsed using

[or constructed from an iterator of](https://docs.rs/struct.PointerBuf.html#method.parse)

`PointerBuf::parse`[s with the](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html)

`Token`[method:](https://docs.rs/struct.PointerBuf.html#method.from_tokens)

`from_tokens````
use jsonptr::PointerBuf;
let mut buf = PointerBuf::parse("/examples/0/name").unwrap();
let from_tokens = PointerBuf::from_tokens(["examples", "0", "name"]);
assert_eq!(&buf, &from_tokens);
buf.push_front("pointer");
buf.push_front("~");
buf.push_back("/");
assert_eq!(buf.as_str(), "/~0/pointer/examples/0/name/~1");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#token-iteration)Token Iteration

Iterating over the tokens or components of a pointer:

```
use jsonptr::{Pointer, Component, Token};
let ptr = Pointer::from_static("/path/to/value");
//  Using the `tokens` method:
let tokens: Vec<_> = ptr.tokens().collect();
assert_eq!(tokens, vec![Token::new("path"), Token::new("to"), Token::new("value")]);
// Using the `components` method:
let mut components = ptr.components();
assert_eq!(components.next(), Some(Component::Root));
assert_eq!(components.next(), Some(Component::Token(Token::new("path"))));
assert_eq!(components.next(), Some(Component::Token(Token::new("to"))));
assert_eq!(components.next(), Some(Component::Token(Token::new("value"))));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#resolving-values)Resolving Values

To get a value at the location of a pointer, use either the [ Resolve](https://docs.rs/resolve/index.html) and

[traits or](https://docs.rs/resolve/trait.ResolveMut.html)

`ResolveMut`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Pointer.html#method.resolve)

`Pointer::resolve`[methods. See the](https://docs.rs/struct.Pointer.html#method.resolve_mut)

`Pointer::resolve_mut`[mod for more information.](https://docs.rs/resolve/index.html)

`resolve````
use jsonptr::Pointer;
use serde_json::json;
let ptr = Pointer::parse("/foo/bar").unwrap();
let data = json!({"foo": { "bar": 34 }});
let bar = ptr.resolve(&data).unwrap();
assert_eq!(bar, &json!(34));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#assigning-values)Assigning Values

Values can be set, with path expansion, using the either the [ Assign](crate::asign) trait or

[. See](https://docs.rs/struct.Pointer.html#method.assign)

`Pointer::assign`[for more information.](crate::asign)

`assign````
use jsonptr::Pointer;
use serde_json::json;
let ptr = Pointer::parse("/secret/universe").unwrap();
let mut data = json!({"secret": { "universe": 42 }});
let replaced = ptr.assign(&mut data, json!(34)).unwrap();
assert_eq!(replaced, Some(json!(42)));
assert_eq!(data, json!({"secret": { "universe": 34 }}));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#deleting-values)Deleting Values

Values can be removed with the either the [ Delete](https://docs.rs/delete/index.html) trait or

[. See](https://docs.rs/struct.Pointer.html#method.delete)

`Pointer::delete`[for more information.](https://docs.rs/delete/index.html)

`delete````
use jsonptr::Pointer;
use serde_json::json;
let ptr = Pointer::parse("/secret/universe").unwrap();
let mut data = json!({"secret": { "universe": 42 }});
let replaced = ptr.assign(&mut data, json!(34)).unwrap();
assert_eq!(replaced, Some(json!(42)));
assert_eq!(data, json!({"secret": { "universe": 34 }}));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#error-reporting)Error Reporting

Any error produced by function calls into methods of traits or types of this
crate can be converted into a [ Report](https://docs.rs/diagnostic/struct.Report.html) which contains the original error
and the

[which failed to parse or the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

`String`[which failed to resolve or assign.](https://docs.rs/struct.PointerBuf.html)

`PointerBuf````
    use jsonptr::{Pointer, Diagnose};
    let ptr_str = "foo/bar";
    let err /* Result<&Pointer, Report<ParseError>> */ = Pointer::parse(ptr_str).diagnose(ptr_str).unwrap_err();
    assert!(err.original().is_no_leading_slash());
```
In the case of [ PointerBuf::parse](https://docs.rs/struct.PointerBuf.html#method.parse), the

[is always wrapped in a](https://docs.rs/enum.ParseError.html)

`ParseError`[so that the input](https://docs.rs/diagnostic/struct.Report.html)

`Report``String` is not dropped.```
    use jsonptr::{PointerBuf};
    let ptr_str = "foo/bar";
    let err /* Result<&PointerBuf, Report<ParseError>> */ = PointerBuf::parse(ptr_str).unwrap_err();
    assert!(err.original().is_no_leading_slash());
```

# jsonptr 0.7.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/jsonptr/latest/source/README.md

```
[<img alt="github" src="https://img.shields.io/badge/github-chanced/jsonptr-62D1FC?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=777&logo=github" height="21">](https://github.com/chanced/jsonptr)
[<img alt="crates.io" src="https://img.shields.io/crates/v/jsonptr.svg?style=for-the-badge&color=fc8d62&logo=rust" height="21">](https://crates.io/crates/jsonptr)
[<img alt="docs.rs" src="https://img.shields.io/badge/docs.rs-jsonptr-f0f0f0?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=777&logo=docs.rs" height="21">](https://docs.rs/jsonptr)
[<img alt="build status" src="https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/chanced/jsonptr/test.yml?branch=main&style=for-the-badge" height="21">](https://github.com/chanced/jsonptr/actions?query=branch%3Amain)
[<img alt="code coverage" src="https://img.shields.io/codecov/c/github/chanced/jsonptr?style=for-the-badge&color=CBB88D" height="21">](https://codecov.io/gh/chanced/jsonptr)
JSON Pointers ([RFC 6901](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6901))
defines a string syntax for identifying a specific location within a JSON, or
similar, document. This crate provides two types, [`Pointer`] and [`PointerBuf`]
(akin to [`Path`] and [`PathBuf`]), for working with them abstractly.
A pointer is composed of zero or more [`Token`]s, single segments which
represent a field of an object or an [`index`] of an array, and are bounded by
either `'/'` or the end of the string. Tokens are lightly encoded, where `'~'`
is escaped as `"~0"` due to it signaling encoding and `'/'` is escaped as `"~1"`
because `'/'` separates tokens and would split the token into two otherwise.
[`Token`]s can be iterated over using either [`Tokens`], returned from the
[`tokens`] method of a pointer or [`Components`], returned from the
[`components`] method. The difference being that `Tokens` iterates over each
token in the pointer, while `Components` iterates over [`Component`]s, which can
represent the root of the document or a single token of the pointer.
Operations [`resolve`], [`assign`] and [`delete`] are provided as traits with
corresponding methods on pointer types. Implementations of each trait are
provided for value types of the crates [`serde_json`] and [`toml`]. All
operations are enabled by default but are gated by [feature
flags](#feature-flags).
To parse a [`Pointer`] from a string, use either [`Pointer::parse`], for
potentially fallible parsing, or the `const fn` `from_static` to produce a
`&'static Pointer` from a string that is known to be valid.
```rust
use jsonptr::Pointer;
let ptr = Pointer::parse("/examples/0/name").unwrap();
let static_ptr = Pointer::from_static("/examples/0/name");
assert_eq!(ptr, static_ptr);
assert_eq!(ptr.get(1..).unwrap(), Pointer::parse("/0/name").unwrap());
let parent = ptr.parent().unwrap();
assert_eq!(parent, Pointer::parse("/examples/0").unwrap());
let (token, remaining) = ptr.split_front().unwrap();
assert_eq!(token.decoded(), "examples");
assert_eq!(remaining, Pointer::parse("/0/name").unwrap());
```
[`PointerBuf`]s can be parsed using [`PointerBuf::parse`] or constructed from an
iterator of [`Token`]s with the [`from_tokens`] method:
```rust
use jsonptr::PointerBuf;
let mut buf = PointerBuf::parse("/examples/0/name").unwrap();
let from_tokens = PointerBuf::from_tokens(["examples", "0", "name"]);
assert_eq!(&buf, &from_tokens);
buf.push_front("pointer");
buf.push_front("~");
buf.push_back("/");
assert_eq!(buf.as_str(), "/~0/pointer/examples/0/name/~1");
```
Iterating over the tokens or components of a pointer:
```rust
use jsonptr::{Pointer, Component, Token};
let ptr = Pointer::from_static("/path/to/value");
//  Using the `tokens` method:
let tokens: Vec<_> = ptr.tokens().collect();
assert_eq!(tokens, vec![Token::new("path"), Token::new("to"), Token::new("value")]);
// Using the `components` method:
let mut components = ptr.components();
assert_eq!(components.next(), Some(Component::Root));
assert_eq!(components.next(), Some(Component::Token(Token::new("path"))));
assert_eq!(components.next(), Some(Component::Token(Token::new("to"))));
assert_eq!(components.next(), Some(Component::Token(Token::new("value"))));
```
To get a value at the location of a pointer, use either the [`Resolve`] and
[`ResolveMut`] traits or [`Pointer::resolve`] and [`Pointer::resolve_mut`]
methods. See the [`resolve`] mod for more information.
```rust
use jsonptr::Pointer;
use serde_json::json;
let ptr = Pointer::parse("/foo/bar").unwrap();
let data = json!({"foo": { "bar": 34 }});
let bar = ptr.resolve(&data).unwrap();
assert_eq!(bar, &json!(34));
```
Values can be set, with path expansion, using the either the [`Assign`] trait or
[`Pointer::assign`]. See [`assign`] for more information.
```rust
use jsonptr::Pointer;
use serde_json::json;
let ptr = Pointer::parse("/secret/universe").unwrap();
let mut data = json!({"secret": { "universe": 42 }});
let replaced = ptr.assign(&mut data, json!(34)).unwrap();
assert_eq!(replaced, Some(json!(42)));
assert_eq!(data, json!({"secret": { "universe": 34 }}));
```
Values can be removed with the either the [`Delete`] trait or
[`Pointer::delete`]. See [`delete`] for more information.
```rust
use jsonptr::Pointer;
use serde_json::json;
let ptr = Pointer::parse("/secret/universe").unwrap();
let mut data = json!({"secret": { "universe": 42 }});
let replaced = ptr.assign(&mut data, json!(34)).unwrap();
assert_eq!(replaced, Some(json!(42)));
assert_eq!(data, json!({"secret": { "universe": 34 }}));
```
Any error produced by function calls into methods of traits or types of this
crate can be converted into a [`Report`] which contains the original error
and the [`String`] which failed to parse or the [`PointerBuf`] which failed to
resolve or assign.
```rust
```
In the case of [`PointerBuf::parse`], the [`ParseError`] is always wrapped in a
[`Report`] so that the input `String` is not dropped.
```rust
```

# serde 1.0.228 - Docs.rs

                    serde 1.0.228

                A generic serialization/deserialization framework

# serde_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_core/=1.0.228/

## Expand description

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The `serde_core` crate contains Serde’s trait definitions with **no support
for #[derive()]**.

In crates that derive an implementation of `Serialize` or `Deserialize`, you
must depend on the [ serde](https://crates.io/crates/serde) crate, not

`serde_core`.In crates that handwrite implementations of Serde traits, or only use them
as trait bounds, depending on `serde_core` is permitted. But `serde`
re-exports all of these traits and can be used for this use case too. If in
doubt, disregard `serde_core` and always use `serde`.

Crates that depend on `serde_core` instead of `serde` are able to compile in
parallel with `serde_derive` even when `serde`’s “derive” feature is turned on,
as shown in the following build timings.

| When `serde_json`depends on`serde` |

| When `serde_json`depends on`serde_core` |

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [forward_](https://docs.rs/macro.forward_to_deserialize_any.html)- to_ - deserialize_ - any
- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/serde/1.0.228/target-redirect/serde/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

# toml - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/toml

## Expand description

A [serde](https://serde.rs/)-compatible [TOML](https://github.com/toml-lang/toml)-parsing library

TOML itself is a simple, ergonomic, and readable configuration format:

```
[package]
name = "toml"
[dependencies]
serde = "1.0"
```
The TOML format tends to be relatively common throughout the Rust community
for configuration, notably being used by [Cargo](https://crates.io/), Rust’s package manager.

[§](https://docs.rs#toml-values)TOML values

A TOML document is represented with the [ Table](https://docs.rs/type.Table.html) type which maps

`String` to the [enum:](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html)

`Value````
pub enum Value {
   String(String),
   Integer(i64),
   Float(f64),
   Boolean(bool),
   Datetime(Datetime),
   Array(Array),
   Table(Table),
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-toml)Parsing TOML

The easiest way to parse a TOML document is via the [ Table](https://docs.rs/type.Table.html) type:

```
use toml::Table;
let value = "foo = 'bar'".parse::<Table>().unwrap();
assert_eq!(value["foo"].as_str(), Some("bar"));
```
The [ Table](https://docs.rs/type.Table.html) type implements a number of convenience methods and
traits; the example above uses

[to parse a](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/traits/trait.FromStr.html)

`FromStr`[into a](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)

`str`[.](https://docs.rs/type.Table.html)

`Table`[§](https://docs.rs#deserialization-and-serialization)Deserialization and Serialization

This crate supports [ serde](https://serde.rs/) 1.0 with a number of
implementations of the

`Deserialize`, `Serialize`, `Deserializer`, and
`Serializer` traits. Namely, you’ll find:- `Deserialize for Table`
- `Serialize for Table`
- `Deserialize for Value`
- `Serialize for Value`
- `Deserialize for Datetime`
- `Serialize for Datetime`
- `Deserializer for de::Deserializer`
- `Serializer for ser::Serializer`
- `Deserializer for Table`
- `Deserializer for Value`

This means that you can use Serde to deserialize/serialize the
[ Table](https://docs.rs/type.Table.html) type as well as

[and](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html)

`Value`[type in this crate. You can also use the](https://docs.rs/value/struct.Datetime.html)

`Datetime`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Deserializer.html)

`Deserializer`[, or](https://docs.rs/struct.Serializer.html)

`Serializer`[type itself to act as a deserializer/serializer for arbitrary types.](https://docs.rs/type.Table.html)

`Table`An example of deserializing with TOML is:

```
use serde::Deserialize;
#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct Config {
   ip: String,
   port: Option<u16>,
   keys: Keys,
}
#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct Keys {
   github: String,
   travis: Option<String>,
}
let config: Config = toml::from_str(r#"
   ip = '127.0.0.1'
   [keys]
   github = 'xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx'
   travis = 'yyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyy'
"#).unwrap();
assert_eq!(config.ip, "127.0.0.1");
assert_eq!(config.port, None);
assert_eq!(config.keys.github, "xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx");
assert_eq!(config.keys.travis.as_ref().unwrap(), "yyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyy");
```
You can serialize types in a similar fashion:

```
use serde::Serialize;
#[derive(Serialize)]
struct Config {
   ip: String,
   port: Option<u16>,
   keys: Keys,
}
#[derive(Serialize)]
struct Keys {
   github: String,
   travis: Option<String>,
}
let config = Config {
   ip: "127.0.0.1".to_string(),
   port: None,
   keys: Keys {
       github: "xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx".to_string(),
       travis: Some("yyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyy".to_string()),
   },
};
let toml = toml::to_string(&config).unwrap();
```
