}## Expand description

A **data format** that can deserialize any data structure supported by
Serde.

The role of this trait is to define the deserialization half of the [Serde
data model](https://serde.rs/data-model.html), which is a way to categorize every Rust data type into one of
29 possible types. Each method of the `Deserializer` trait corresponds to one
of the types of the data model.

Implementations of `Deserialize` map themselves into this data model by
passing to the `Deserializer` a `Visitor` implementation that can receive
these various types.

The types that make up the Serde data model are:

- **14 primitive types**- bool
- i8, i16, i32, i64, i128
- u8, u16, u32, u64, u128
- f32, f64
- char

- **string**- UTF-8 bytes with a length and no null terminator.
- When serializing, all strings are handled equally. When deserializing, there are three flavors of strings: transient, owned, and borrowed.

- **byte array**- [u8]- Similar to strings, during deserialization byte arrays can be transient, owned, or borrowed.

- **option**- Either none or some value.

- **unit**- The type of `()`in Rust. It represents an anonymous value containing no data.

- The type of
- **unit_struct**- For example `struct Unit`or`PhantomData<T>`. It represents a named value containing no data.

- For example
- **unit_variant**- For example the `E::A`and`E::B`in`enum E { A, B }`.

- For example the
- **newtype_struct**- For example `struct Millimeters(u8)`.

- For example
- **newtype_variant**- For example the `E::N`in`enum E { N(u8) }`.

- For example the
- **seq**- A variably sized heterogeneous sequence of values, for example `Vec<T>`or`HashSet<T>`. When serializing, the length may or may not be known before iterating through all the data. When deserializing, the length is determined by looking at the serialized data.

- A variably sized heterogeneous sequence of values, for example
- **tuple**- A statically sized heterogeneous sequence of values for which the
length will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example `(u8,)`or`(String, u64, Vec<T>)`or`[u64; 10]`.

- A statically sized heterogeneous sequence of values for which the
length will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example
- **tuple_struct**- A named tuple, for example `struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8)`.

- A named tuple, for example
- **tuple_variant**- For example the `E::T`in`enum E { T(u8, u8) }`.

- For example the
- **map**- A heterogeneous key-value pairing, for example `BTreeMap<K, V>`.

- A heterogeneous key-value pairing, for example
- **struct**- A heterogeneous key-value pairing in which the keys are strings and
will be known at deserialization time without looking at the serialized
data, for example `struct S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 }`.

- A heterogeneous key-value pairing in which the keys are strings and
will be known at deserialization time without looking at the serialized
data, for example
- **struct_variant**- For example the `E::S`in`enum E { S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 } }`.

- For example the

The `Deserializer` trait supports two entry point styles which enables
different kinds of deserialization.

-
The `deserialize_any`method. Self-describing data formats like JSON are able to look at the serialized data and tell what it represents. For example the JSON deserializer may see an opening curly brace (`{`) and know that it is seeing a map. If the data format supports`Deserializer::deserialize_any`, it will drive the Visitor using whatever type it sees in the input. JSON uses this approach when deserializing`serde_json::Value`which is an enum that can represent any JSON document. Without knowing what is in a JSON document, we can deserialize it to`serde_json::Value`by going through`Deserializer::deserialize_any`.
-
The various `deserialize_*`methods. Non-self-describing formats like Postcard need to be told what is in the input in order to deserialize it. The`deserialize_*`methods are hints to the deserializer for how to interpret the next piece of input. Non-self-describing formats are not able to deserialize something like`serde_json::Value`which relies on`Deserializer::deserialize_any`.

When implementing `Deserialize`, you should avoid relying on
`Deserializer::deserialize_any` unless you need to be told by the
Deserializer what type is in the input. Know that relying on
`Deserializer::deserialize_any` means your data type will be able to
deserialize from self-describing formats only, ruling out Postcard and many
others.

[§](https://docs.rs#lifetime)Lifetime

The `'de` lifetime of this trait is the lifetime of data that may be
borrowed from the input when deserializing. See the page [Understanding
deserializer lifetimes](https://serde.rs/lifetimes.html) for a more detailed explanation of these lifetimes.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-implementation)Example implementation

The [example data format](https://serde.rs/data-format.html) presented on the website contains example code for
a basic JSON `Deserializer`.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_core/de/mod.rs.html#1253-1255)#### fn [is_human_readable](https://docs.rs#method.is_human_readable)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_core/de/mod.rs.html#1253-1255)

#### fn [is_human_readable](https://docs.rs#method.is_human_readable)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.bool.html)

Determine whether `Deserialize` implementations should expect to
deserialize their human-readable form.

Some types have a human-readable form that may be somewhat expensive to construct, as well as a binary form that is compact and efficient. Generally text-based formats like JSON and YAML will prefer to use the human-readable one and binary formats like Postcard will prefer the compact one.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::de::{self, Deserialize, Deserializer};
impl<'de> Deserialize<'de> for Timestamp {
    fn deserialize<D>(deserializer: D) -> Result<Self, D::Error>
    where
        D: Deserializer<'de>,
    {
        if deserializer.is_human_readable() {
            // Deserialize from a human-readable string like "2015-05-15T17:01:00Z".
            let s = String::deserialize(deserializer)?;
            Timestamp::from_str(&s).map_err(de::Error::custom)
        } else {
            // Deserialize from a compact binary representation, seconds since
            // the Unix epoch.
            let n = u64::deserialize(deserializer)?;
            Ok(Timestamp::EPOCH + Duration::seconds(n))
        }
    }
}
```
The default implementation of this method returns `true`. Data formats
may override this to `false` to request a compact form for types that
support one. Note that modifying this method to change a format from
human-readable to compact or vice versa should be regarded as a breaking
change, as a value serialized in human-readable mode is not required to
deserialize from the same data in compact mode.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# Error in serde_json - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_json/1.0/serde_json/struct.Error.html

`pub struct Error { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

This type represents all possible errors that can occur when serializing or deserializing JSON data.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

One-based line number at which the error was detected.

Characters in the first line of the input (before the first newline character) are in line 1.

One-based column number at which the error was detected.

The first character in the input and any characters immediately following a newline character are in column 1.

Note that errors may occur in column 0, for example if a read from an I/O stream fails immediately following a previously read newline character.

Categorizes the cause of this error.

- `Category::Io`- failure to read or write bytes on an I/O stream
- `Category::Syntax`- input that is not syntactically valid JSON
- `Category::Data`- input data that is semantically incorrect
- `Category::Eof`- unexpected end of the input data

Returns true if this error was caused by a failure to read or write bytes on an I/O stream.

Returns true if this error was caused by input that was not syntactically valid JSON.

Returns true if this error was caused by input data that was semantically incorrect.

For example, JSON containing a number is semantically incorrect when the type being deserialized into holds a String.

Returns true if this error was caused by prematurely reaching the end of the input data.

Callers that process streaming input may be interested in retrying the deserialization once more data is available.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_json/error.rs.html#155-161)#### pub fn [io_error_kind](https://docs.rs#method.io_error_kind)(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[ErrorKind](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/io/error/enum.ErrorKind.html)>

**crate feature **`std` only.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_json/error.rs.html#155-161)

#### pub fn [io_error_kind](https://docs.rs#method.io_error_kind)(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[ErrorKind](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/io/error/enum.ErrorKind.html)>

**crate feature**only.

`std`The kind reported by the underlying standard library I/O error, if this error was caused by a failure to read or write bytes on an I/O stream.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use serde_json::Value;
use std::io::{self, ErrorKind, Read};
use std::process;
struct ReaderThatWillTimeOut<'a>(&'a [u8]);
impl<'a> Read for ReaderThatWillTimeOut<'a> {
    fn read(&mut self, buf: &mut [u8]) -> io::Result<usize> {
        if self.0.is_empty() {
            Err(io::Error::new(ErrorKind::TimedOut, "timed out"))
        } else {
            self.0.read(buf)
        }
    }
}
fn main() {
    let reader = ReaderThatWillTimeOut(br#" {"k": "#);
    let _: Value = match serde_json::from_reader(reader) {
        Ok(value) => value,
        Err(error) => {
            if error.io_error_kind() == Some(ErrorKind::TimedOut) {
                // Maybe this application needs to retry certain kinds of errors.
            } else {
                eprintln!("error: {}", error);
                process::exit(1);
            }
        }
    };
}
```

`Deserialize` struct type received a field with an
unrecognized name.Convert a `serde_json::Error` into an `io::Error`.

JSON syntax and data errors are turned into `InvalidData` I/O errors.
EOF errors are turned into `UnexpectedEof` I/O errors.

```
use std::io;
enum MyError {
    Io(io::Error),
    Json(serde_json::Error),
}
impl From<serde_json::Error> for MyError {
    fn from(err: serde_json::Error) -> MyError {
        use serde_json::error::Category;
        match err.classify() {
            Category::Io => {
                MyError::Io(err.into())
            }
            Category::Syntax | Category::Data | Category::Eof => {
                MyError::Json(err)
            }
        }
    }
}
```

       where A: [EnumAccess](https://docs.rs/trait.EnumAccess.html)<'de> { ... }
}## Expand description

This trait represents a visitor that walks through a deserializer.

[§](https://docs.rs#lifetime)Lifetime

The `'de` lifetime of this trait is the requirement for lifetime of data
that may be borrowed by `Self::Value`. See the page [Understanding
deserializer lifetimes](https://serde.rs/lifetimes.html) for a more detailed explanation of these lifetimes.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
/// A visitor that deserializes a long string - a string containing at least
/// some minimum number of bytes.
struct LongString {
    min: usize,
}
impl<'de> Visitor<'de> for LongString {
    type Value = String;
    fn expecting(&self, formatter: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
        write!(formatter, "a string containing at least {} bytes", self.min)
    }
    fn visit_str<E>(self, s: &str) -> Result<Self::Value, E>
    where
        E: de::Error,
    {
        if s.len() >= self.min {
            Ok(s.to_owned())
        } else {
            Err(de::Error::invalid_value(Unexpected::Str(s), &self))
        }
    }
}
```
## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Format a message stating what data this Visitor expects to receive.

This is used in error messages. The message should complete the sentence “This Visitor expects to receive …”, for example the message could be “an integer between 0 and 64”. The message should not be capitalized and should not end with a period.

The input contains a string. The lifetime of the string is ephemeral and it may be destroyed after this method returns.

This method allows the `Deserializer` to avoid a copy by retaining
ownership of any buffered data. `Deserialize` implementations that do
not benefit from taking ownership of `String` data should indicate that
to the deserializer by using `Deserializer::deserialize_str` rather than
`Deserializer::deserialize_string`.

It is never correct to implement `visit_string` without implementing
`visit_str`. Implement neither, both, or just `visit_str`.

The input contains a string that lives at least as long as the
`Deserializer`.

This enables zero-copy deserialization of strings in some formats. For
example JSON input containing the JSON string `"borrowed"` can be
deserialized with zero copying into a `&'a str` as long as the input
data outlives `'a`.

The default implementation forwards to `visit_str`.

# mod.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/serde_core/de/mod.rs.html

# serde_core/de/mod.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! Generic data structure deserialization framework.
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! The two most important traits in this module are [`Deserialize`] and
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! [`Deserializer`].
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//!
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//!  - **A type that implements `Deserialize` is a data structure** that can be
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//!    deserialized from any data format supported by Serde, and conversely
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!  - **A type that implements `Deserializer` is a data format** that can
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//!    deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! # The Deserialize trait
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! Serde provides [`Deserialize`] implementations for many Rust primitive and
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! standard library types. The complete list is below. All of these can be
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! deserialized using Serde out of the box.
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! Additionally, Serde provides a procedural macro called [`serde_derive`] to
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! automatically generate [`Deserialize`] implementations for structs and enums
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! in your program. See the [derive section of the manual] for how to use this.
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! In rare cases it may be necessary to implement [`Deserialize`] manually for
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! some type in your program. See the [Implementing `Deserialize`] section of
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! the manual for more about this.
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//!
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! Third-party crates may provide [`Deserialize`] implementations for types
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! that they expose. For example the [`linked-hash-map`] crate provides a
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! [`LinkedHashMap<K, V>`] type that is deserializable by Serde because the
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! crate provides an implementation of [`Deserialize`] for it.
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! # The Deserializer trait
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! [`Deserializer`] implementations are provided by third-party crates, for
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! example [`serde_json`], [`serde_yaml`] and [`postcard`].
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//!
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! A partial list of well-maintained formats is given on the [Serde
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! website][data formats].
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//!
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! # Implementations of Deserialize provided by Serde
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//!
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! This is a slightly different set of types than what is supported for
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! serialization. Some types can be serialized by Serde but not deserialized.
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! One example is `OsStr`.
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!  - **Primitive types**:
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//!    - bool
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!    - i8, i16, i32, i64, i128, isize
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!    - u8, u16, u32, u64, u128, usize
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!    - f32, f64
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!    - char
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!  - **Compound types**:

[137](https://docs.rs#137)macro_rules! declare_error_trait {
[138](https://docs.rs#138)    (Error: Sized $(+ $($supertrait:ident)::+)*) => {
[139](https://docs.rs#139)        /// The `Error` trait allows `Deserialize` implementations to create descriptive
[140](https://docs.rs#140)        /// error messages belonging to the `Deserializer` against which they are
[141](https://docs.rs#141)        /// currently running.
[142](https://docs.rs#142)        ///
[143](https://docs.rs#143)        /// Every `Deserializer` declares an `Error` type that encompasses both
[144](https://docs.rs#144)        /// general-purpose deserialization errors as well as errors specific to the
[145](https://docs.rs#145)        /// particular deserialization format. For example the `Error` type of
[146](https://docs.rs#146)        /// `serde_json` can represent errors like an invalid JSON escape sequence or an
[147](https://docs.rs#147)        /// unterminated string literal, in addition to the error cases that are part of
[148](https://docs.rs#148)        /// this trait.
[149](https://docs.rs#149)        ///
[150](https://docs.rs#150)        /// Most deserializers should only need to provide the `Error::custom` method
[151](https://docs.rs#151)        /// and inherit the default behavior for the other methods.
[152](https://docs.rs#152)        ///
[153](https://docs.rs#153)        /// # Example implementation
[154](https://docs.rs#154)        ///
[155](https://docs.rs#155)        /// The [example data format] presented on the website shows an error
[156](https://docs.rs#156)        /// type appropriate for a basic JSON data format.
[157](https://docs.rs#157)        ///
[158](https://docs.rs#158)        /// [example data format]: https://serde.rs/data-format.html
[159](https://docs.rs#159)        #[cfg_attr(
[160](https://docs.rs#160)            not(no_diagnostic_namespace),
[161](https://docs.rs#161)            diagnostic::on_unimplemented(
[162](https://docs.rs#162)                message = "the trait bound `{Self}: serde::de::Error` is not satisfied",
[163](https://docs.rs#163)            )
[164](https://docs.rs#164)        )]
[165](https://docs.rs#165)        pub trait [Error](https://docs.rs/serde_core/de/trait.Error.html): Sized $(+ $($supertrait)::+)* {
[166](https://docs.rs#166)            /// Raised when there is general error when deserializing a type.
[167](https://docs.rs#167)            ///
[168](https://docs.rs#168)            /// The message should not be capitalized and should not end with a period.
[169](https://docs.rs#169)            ///
[170](https://docs.rs#170)            /// ```edition2021
[171](https://docs.rs#171)            /// # use std::str::FromStr;
[172](https://docs.rs#172)            /// #
[173](https://docs.rs#173)            /// # struct IpAddr;
[174](https://docs.rs#174)            /// #
[175](https://docs.rs#175)            /// # impl FromStr for IpAddr {
[176](https://docs.rs#176)            /// #     type Err = String;
[177](https://docs.rs#177)            /// #
[178](https://docs.rs#178)            /// #     fn from_str(_: &str) -> Result<Self, String> {
[179](https://docs.rs#179)            /// #         unimplemented!()
[180](https://docs.rs#180)            /// #     }
[181](https://docs.rs#181)            /// # }
[182](https://docs.rs#182)            /// #
[183](https://docs.rs#183)            /// use serde::de::{self, Deserialize, Deserializer};
[184](https://docs.rs#184)            ///
[185](https://docs.rs#185)            /// impl<'de> Deserialize<'de> for IpAddr {
[186](https://docs.rs#186)            ///     fn deserialize<D>(deserializer: D) -> Result<Self, D::Error>
[187](https://docs.rs#187)            ///     where
[188](https://docs.rs#188)            ///         D: Deserializer<'de>,
[189](https://docs.rs#189)            ///     {
[190](https://docs.rs#190)            ///         let s = String::deserialize(deserializer)?;
[191](https://docs.rs#191)            ///         s.parse().map_err(de::Error::custom)
[192](https://docs.rs#192)            ///     }
[193](https://docs.rs#193)            /// }
[194](https://docs.rs#194)            /// ```
[195](https://docs.rs#195)            fn custom<T>(msg: T) -> Self
[196](https://docs.rs#196)            where
[197](https://docs.rs#197)                T: Display;
[198](https://docs.rs#198)
[199](https://docs.rs#199)            /// Raised when a `Deserialize` receives a type different from what it was
[200](https://docs.rs#200)            /// expecting.
[201](https://docs.rs#201)            ///
[202](https://docs.rs#202)            /// The `unexp` argument provides information about what type was received.
[203](https://docs.rs#203)            /// This is the type that was present in the input file or other source data
[204](https://docs.rs#204)            /// of the Deserializer.
[205](https://docs.rs#205)            ///
[206](https://docs.rs#206)            /// The `exp` argument provides information about what type was being
[207](https://docs.rs#207)            /// expected. This is the type that is written in the program.
[208](https://docs.rs#208)            ///
[209](https://docs.rs#209)            /// For example if we try to deserialize a String out of a JSON file
[210](https://docs.rs#210)            /// containing an integer, the unexpected type is the integer and the
[211](https://docs.rs#211)            /// expected type is the string.
[212](https://docs.rs#212)            #[cold]
[213](https://docs.rs#213)            fn invalid_type(unexp: [Unexpected](https://docs.rs#338-399), exp: &dyn Expected) -> Self {
[214](https://docs.rs#214)                Error::custom(format_args!("invalid type: {}, expected {}", unexp, exp))
[215](https://docs.rs#215)            }
[216](https://docs.rs#216)
[217](https://docs.rs#217)            /// Raised when a `Deserialize` receives a value of the right type but that
[218](https://docs.rs#218)            /// is wrong for some other reason.
[219](https://docs.rs#219)            ///
[220](https://docs.rs#220)            /// The `unexp` argument provides information about what value was received.
[221](https://docs.rs#221)            /// This is the value that was present in the input file or other source
[222](https://docs.rs#222)            /// data of the Deserializer.
[223](https://docs.rs#223)            ///
[224](https://docs.rs#224)            /// The `exp` argument provides information about what value was being
[225](https://docs.rs#225)            /// expected. This is the type that is written in the program.
[226](https://docs.rs#226)            ///
[227](https://docs.rs#227)            /// For example if we try to deserialize a String out of some binary data
[228](https://docs.rs#228)            /// that is not valid UTF-8, the unexpected value is the bytes and the
[229](https://docs.rs#229)            /// expected value is a string.
[230](https://docs.rs#230)            #[cold]
[231](https://docs.rs#231)            fn invalid_value(unexp: [Unexpected](https://docs.rs#338-399), exp: &dyn Expected) -> Self {
[232](https://docs.rs#232)                Error::custom(format_args!("invalid value: {}, expected {}", unexp, exp))
[233](https://docs.rs#233)            }
[234](https://docs.rs#234)
[235](https://docs.rs#235)            /// Raised when deserializing a sequence or map and the input data contains
[236](https://docs.rs#236)            /// too many or too few elements.
[237](https://docs.rs#237)            ///
[238](https://docs.rs#238)            /// The `len` argument is the number of elements encountered. The sequence
[239](https://docs.rs#239)            /// or map may have expected more arguments or fewer arguments.
[240](https://docs.rs#240)            ///
[241](https://docs.rs#241)            /// The `exp` argument provides information about what data was being
[242](https://docs.rs#242)            /// expected. For example `exp` might say that a tuple of size 6 was
[243](https://docs.rs#243)            /// expected.
[244](https://docs.rs#244)            #[cold]
[245](https://docs.rs#245)            fn invalid_length(len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html), exp: &dyn Expected) -> Self {
[246](https://docs.rs#246)                Error::custom(format_args!("invalid length {}, expected {}", len, exp))
[247](https://docs.rs#247)            }
[248](https://docs.rs#248)
[249](https://docs.rs#249)            /// Raised when a `Deserialize` enum type received a variant with an
[250](https://docs.rs#250)            /// unrecognized name.
[251](https://docs.rs#251)            #[cold]
[252](https://docs.rs#252)            fn unknown_variant(variant: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html), expected: &'static [&'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html)]) -> Self {
[253](https://docs.rs#253)                if expected.is_empty() {
[254](https://docs.rs#254)                    Error::custom(format_args!(
[255](https://docs.rs#255)                        "unknown variant `{}`, there are no variants",
[256](https://docs.rs#256)                        variant
[257](https://docs.rs#257)                    ))
[258](https://docs.rs#258)                } else {
[259](https://docs.rs#259)                    Error::custom(format_args!(
[260](https://docs.rs#260)                        "unknown variant `{}`, expected {}",
[261](https://docs.rs#261)                        variant,
[262](https://docs.rs#262)                        OneOf { names: expected }
[263](https://docs.rs#263)                    ))
[264](https://docs.rs#264)                }
[265](https://docs.rs#265)            }
[266](https://docs.rs#266)
[267](https://docs.rs#267)            /// Raised when a `Deserialize` struct type received a field with an
[268](https://docs.rs#268)            /// unrecognized name.
[269](https://docs.rs#269)            #[cold]
[270](https://docs.rs#270)            fn unknown_field(field: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html), expected: &'static [&'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html)]) -> Self {
[271](https://docs.rs#271)                if expected.is_empty() {
[272](https://docs.rs#272)                    Error::custom(format_args!(
[273](https://docs.rs#273)                        "unknown field `{}`, there are no fields",
[274](https://docs.rs#274)                        field
[275](https://docs.rs#275)                    ))
[276](https://docs.rs#276)                } else {
[277](https://docs.rs#277)                    Error::custom(format_args!(
[278](https://docs.rs#278)                        "unknown field `{}`, expected {}",
[279](https://docs.rs#279)                        field,
[280](https://docs.rs#280)                        OneOf { names: expected }
[281](https://docs.rs#281)                    ))
[282](https://docs.rs#282)                }
[283](https://docs.rs#283)            }
[284](https://docs.rs#284)
[285](https://docs.rs#285)            /// Raised when a `Deserialize` struct type expected to receive a required
[286](https://docs.rs#286)            /// field with a particular name but that field was not present in the
[287](https://docs.rs#287)            /// input.
[288](https://docs.rs#288)            #[cold]
[289](https://docs.rs#289)            fn missing_field(field: &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html)) -> Self {
[290](https://docs.rs#290)                Error::custom(format_args!("missing field `{}`", field))
[291](https://docs.rs#291)            }
[292](https://docs.rs#292)
[293](https://docs.rs#293)            /// Raised when a `Deserialize` struct type received more than one of the
[294](https://docs.rs#294)            /// same field.
[295](https://docs.rs#295)            #[cold]
[296](https://docs.rs#296)            fn duplicate_field(field: &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html)) -> Self {
[297](https://docs.rs#297)                Error::custom(format_args!("duplicate field `{}`", field))
[298](https://docs.rs#298)            }
[299](https://docs.rs#299)        }
[300](https://docs.rs#300)    }
[301](https://docs.rs#301)}

[307](https://docs.rs#307)declare_error_trait!(Error: Sized + Debug + Display);
[308](https://docs.rs#308)
[309](https://docs.rs#309)/// `Unexpected` represents an unexpected invocation of any one of the `Visitor`
[310](https://docs.rs#310)/// trait methods.
[311](https://docs.rs#311)///
[312](https://docs.rs#312)/// This is used as an argument to the `invalid_type`, `invalid_value`, and
[313](https://docs.rs#313)/// `invalid_length` methods of the `Error` trait to build error messages.
[314](https://docs.rs#314)///
[315](https://docs.rs#315)/// ```edition2021
[316](https://docs.rs#316)/// # use std::fmt;
[317](https://docs.rs#317)/// #
[318](https://docs.rs#318)/// # use serde::de::{self, Unexpected, Visitor};
[319](https://docs.rs#319)/// #
[320](https://docs.rs#320)/// # struct Example;
[321](https://docs.rs#321)/// #
[322](https://docs.rs#322)/// # impl<'de> Visitor<'de> for Example {
[323](https://docs.rs#323)/// #     type Value = ();
[324](https://docs.rs#324)/// #
[325](https://docs.rs#325)/// #     fn expecting(&self, formatter: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
[326](https://docs.rs#326)/// #         write!(formatter, "definitely not a boolean")
[327](https://docs.rs#327)/// #     }
[328](https://docs.rs#328)/// #
[329](https://docs.rs#329)/// fn visit_bool<E>(self, v: bool) -> Result<Self::Value, E>
[330](https://docs.rs#330)/// where
[331](https://docs.rs#331)///     E: de::Error,
[332](https://docs.rs#332)/// {
[333](https://docs.rs#333)///     Err(de::Error::invalid_type(Unexpected::Bool(v), &self))
[334](https://docs.rs#334)/// }
[335](https://docs.rs#335)/// # }
[336](https://docs.rs#336)/// ```
[337](https://docs.rs#337)#[derive([Copy](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/marker/derive.Copy.html), [Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/clone/derive.Clone.html), [PartialEq](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/cmp/derive.PartialEq.html), [Debug](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/fmt/macros/derive.Debug.html))]
[338](https://docs.rs#338)pub enum [Unexpected](https://docs.rs#338-399)<'a> {
[339](https://docs.rs#339)    /// The input contained a boolean value that was not expected.
[340](https://docs.rs#340)    Bool([bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.bool.html)),
[341](https://docs.rs#341)
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    /// The input contained an unsigned integer `u8`, `u16`, `u32` or `u64` that
[343](https://docs.rs#343)    /// was not expected.
[344](https://docs.rs#344)    Unsigned([u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.u64.html)),
[345](https://docs.rs#345)
[346](https://docs.rs#346)    /// The input contained a signed integer `i8`, `i16`, `i32` or `i64` that
[347](https://docs.rs#347)    /// was not expected.
[348](https://docs.rs#348)    Signed([i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.i64.html)),
[349](https://docs.rs#349)
[350](https://docs.rs#350)    /// The input contained a floating point `f32` or `f64` that was not
[351](https://docs.rs#351)    /// expected.
[352](https://docs.rs#352)    Float([f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.f64.html)),
[353](https://docs.rs#353)
[354](https://docs.rs#354)    /// The input contained a `char` that was not expected.
[355](https://docs.rs#355)    Char([char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.char.html)),
[356](https://docs.rs#356)
[357](https://docs.rs#357)    /// The input contained a `&str` or `String` that was not expected.
[358](https://docs.rs#358)    Str(&'a [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html)),
[359](https://docs.rs#359)
[360](https://docs.rs#360)    /// The input contained a `&[u8]` or `Vec<u8>` that was not expected.
[361](https://docs.rs#361)    Bytes(&'a [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.u8.html)]),
[362](https://docs.rs#362)
[363](https://docs.rs#363)    /// The input contained a unit `()` that was not expected.
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    Unit,
[365](https://docs.rs#365)
[366](https://docs.rs#366)    /// The input contained an `Option<T>` that was not expected.
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    Option,
[368](https://docs.rs#368)
[369](https://docs.rs#369)    /// The input contained a newtype struct that was not expected.
[370](https://docs.rs#370)    NewtypeStruct,
[371](https://docs.rs#371)
[372](https://docs.rs#372)    /// The input contained a sequence that was not expected.
[373](https://docs.rs#373)    Seq,
[374](https://docs.rs#374)
[375](https://docs.rs#375)    /// The input contained a map that was not expected.
[376](https://docs.rs#376)    Map,
[377](https://docs.rs#377)
[378](https://docs.rs#378)    /// The input contained an enum that was not expected.
[379](https://docs.rs#379)    Enum,
[380](https://docs.rs#380)
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    /// The input contained a unit variant that was not expected.
[382](https://docs.rs#382)    UnitVariant,
[383](https://docs.rs#383)
[384](https://docs.rs#384)    /// The input contained a newtype variant that was not expected.
[385](https://docs.rs#385)    NewtypeVariant,
[386](https://docs.rs#386)
[387](https://docs.rs#387)    /// The input contained a tuple variant that was not expected.
[388](https://docs.rs#388)    TupleVariant,
[389](https://docs.rs#389)
[390](https://docs.rs#390)    /// The input contained a struct variant that was not expected.
[391](https://docs.rs#391)    StructVariant,
[392](https://docs.rs#392)
[393](https://docs.rs#393)    /// A message stating what uncategorized thing the input contained that was
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    /// not expected.
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    ///
[396](https://docs.rs#396)    /// The message should be a noun or noun phrase, not capitalized and without

[427](https://docs.rs#427)/// `Expected` represents an explanation of what data a `Visitor` was expecting
[428](https://docs.rs#428)/// to receive.
[429](https://docs.rs#429)///
[430](https://docs.rs#430)/// This is used as an argument to the `invalid_type`, `invalid_value`, and
[431](https://docs.rs#431)/// `invalid_length` methods of the `Error` trait to build error messages. The
[432](https://docs.rs#432)/// message should be a noun or noun phrase that completes the sentence "This
[433](https://docs.rs#433)/// Visitor expects to receive ...", for example the message could be "an
[434](https://docs.rs#434)/// integer between 0 and 64". The message should not be capitalized and should
[435](https://docs.rs#435)/// not end with a period.
[436](https://docs.rs#436)///
[437](https://docs.rs#437)/// Within the context of a `Visitor` implementation, the `Visitor` itself
[438](https://docs.rs#438)/// (`&self`) is an implementation of this trait.
[439](https://docs.rs#439)///
[440](https://docs.rs#440)/// ```edition2021
[441](https://docs.rs#441)/// # use serde::de::{self, Unexpected, Visitor};
[442](https://docs.rs#442)/// # use std::fmt;
[443](https://docs.rs#443)/// #
[444](https://docs.rs#444)/// # struct Example;
[445](https://docs.rs#445)/// #
[446](https://docs.rs#446)/// # impl<'de> Visitor<'de> for Example {
[447](https://docs.rs#447)/// #     type Value = ();
[448](https://docs.rs#448)/// #
[449](https://docs.rs#449)/// #     fn expecting(&self, formatter: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
[450](https://docs.rs#450)/// #         write!(formatter, "definitely not a boolean")
[451](https://docs.rs#451)/// #     }
[452](https://docs.rs#452)/// #
[453](https://docs.rs#453)/// fn visit_bool<E>(self, v: bool) -> Result<Self::Value, E>
[454](https://docs.rs#454)/// where
[455](https://docs.rs#455)///     E: de::Error,
[456](https://docs.rs#456)/// {
[457](https://docs.rs#457)///     Err(de::Error::invalid_type(Unexpected::Bool(v), &self))
[458](https://docs.rs#458)/// }
[459](https://docs.rs#459)/// # }
[460](https://docs.rs#460)/// ```
[461](https://docs.rs#461)///
[462](https://docs.rs#462)/// Outside of a `Visitor`, `&"..."` can be used.
[463](https://docs.rs#463)///
[464](https://docs.rs#464)/// ```edition2021
[465](https://docs.rs#465)/// # use serde::de::{self, Unexpected};
[466](https://docs.rs#466)/// #
[467](https://docs.rs#467)/// # fn example<E>() -> Result<(), E>
[468](https://docs.rs#468)/// # where
[469](https://docs.rs#469)/// #     E: de::Error,
[470](https://docs.rs#470)/// # {
[471](https://docs.rs#471)/// #     let v = true;
[472](https://docs.rs#472)/// return Err(de::Error::invalid_type(
[473](https://docs.rs#473)///     Unexpected::Bool(v),
[474](https://docs.rs#474)///     &"a negative integer",
[475](https://docs.rs#475)/// ));
[476](https://docs.rs#476)/// # }
[477](https://docs.rs#477)/// ```
[478](https://docs.rs#478)#[cfg_attr(
[479](https://docs.rs#479)    not(no_diagnostic_namespace),
[480](https://docs.rs#480)    diagnostic::on_unimplemented(
[481](https://docs.rs#481)        message = "the trait bound `{Self}: serde::de::Expected` is not satisfied",
[482](https://docs.rs#482)    )
[483](https://docs.rs#483))]

[512](https://docs.rs#512)
[513](https://docs.rs#513)/// A **data structure** that can be deserialized from any data format supported
[514](https://docs.rs#514)/// by Serde.
[515](https://docs.rs#515)///
[516](https://docs.rs#516)/// Serde provides `Deserialize` implementations for many Rust primitive and
[517](https://docs.rs#517)/// standard library types. The complete list is [here][crate::de]. All of these
[518](https://docs.rs#518)/// can be deserialized using Serde out of the box.
[519](https://docs.rs#519)///
[520](https://docs.rs#520)/// Additionally, Serde provides a procedural macro called `serde_derive` to
[521](https://docs.rs#521)/// automatically generate `Deserialize` implementations for structs and enums
[522](https://docs.rs#522)/// in your program. See the [derive section of the manual][derive] for how to
[523](https://docs.rs#523)/// use this.
[524](https://docs.rs#524)///
[525](https://docs.rs#525)/// In rare cases it may be necessary to implement `Deserialize` manually for
[526](https://docs.rs#526)/// some type in your program. See the [Implementing
[527](https://docs.rs#527)/// `Deserialize`][impl-deserialize] section of the manual for more about this.
[528](https://docs.rs#528)///
[529](https://docs.rs#529)/// Third-party crates may provide `Deserialize` implementations for types that
[530](https://docs.rs#530)/// they expose. For example the `linked-hash-map` crate provides a
[531](https://docs.rs#531)/// `LinkedHashMap<K, V>` type that is deserializable by Serde because the crate
[532](https://docs.rs#532)/// provides an implementation of `Deserialize` for it.
[533](https://docs.rs#533)///
[534](https://docs.rs#534)/// [derive]: https://serde.rs/derive.html
[535](https://docs.rs#535)/// [impl-deserialize]: https://serde.rs/impl-deserialize.html
[536](https://docs.rs#536)///
[537](https://docs.rs#537)/// # Lifetime
[538](https://docs.rs#538)///
[539](https://docs.rs#539)/// The `'de` lifetime of this trait is the lifetime of data that may be
[540](https://docs.rs#540)/// borrowed by `Self` when deserialized. See the page [Understanding
[541](https://docs.rs#541)/// deserializer lifetimes] for a more detailed explanation of these lifetimes.
[542](https://docs.rs#542)///
[543](https://docs.rs#543)/// [Understanding deserializer lifetimes]: https://serde.rs/lifetimes.html
[544](https://docs.rs#544)#[cfg_attr(
[545](https://docs.rs#545)    not(no_diagnostic_namespace),
[546](https://docs.rs#546)    diagnostic::on_unimplemented(
[547](https://docs.rs#547)        // Prevents `serde_core::de::Deserialize` appearing in the error message
[548](https://docs.rs#548)        // in projects with no direct dependency on serde_core.
[549](https://docs.rs#549)        message = "the trait bound `{Self}: serde::Deserialize<'de>` is not satisfied",
[550](https://docs.rs#550)        note = "for local types consider adding `#[derive(serde::Deserialize)]` to your `{Self}` type",
[551](https://docs.rs#551)        note = "for types from other crates check whether the crate offers a `serde` feature flag",
[552](https://docs.rs#552)    )
[553](https://docs.rs#553))]
[554](https://docs.rs#554)pub trait [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/serde_core/trait.Deserialize.html)<'de>: [Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) {
[555](https://docs.rs#555)    /// Deserialize this value from the given Serde deserializer.
[556](https://docs.rs#556)    ///
[557](https://docs.rs#557)    /// See the [Implementing `Deserialize`][impl-deserialize] section of the
[558](https://docs.rs#558)    /// manual for more information about how to implement this method.
[559](https://docs.rs#559)    ///
[560](https://docs.rs#560)    /// [impl-deserialize]: https://serde.rs/impl-deserialize.html
[561](https://docs.rs#561)    fn deserialize<D>(deserializer: D) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self, D::Error>
[562](https://docs.rs#562)    where
[563](https://docs.rs#563)        D: [Deserializer](https://docs.rs#945-1266)<'de>;
[564](https://docs.rs#564)
[565](https://docs.rs#565)    /// Deserializes a value into `self` from the given Deserializer.
[566](https://docs.rs#566)    ///
[567](https://docs.rs#567)    /// The purpose of this method is to allow the deserializer to reuse
[568](https://docs.rs#568)    /// resources and avoid copies. As such, if this method returns an error,
[569](https://docs.rs#569)    /// `self` will be in an indeterminate state where some parts of the struct
[570](https://docs.rs#570)    /// have been overwritten. Although whatever state that is will be
[571](https://docs.rs#571)    /// memory-safe.
[572](https://docs.rs#572)    ///
[573](https://docs.rs#573)    /// This is generally useful when repeatedly deserializing values that
[574](https://docs.rs#574)    /// are processed one at a time, where the value of `self` doesn't matter
[575](https://docs.rs#575)    /// when the next deserialization occurs.
[576](https://docs.rs#576)    ///
[577](https://docs.rs#577)    /// If you manually implement this, your recursive deserializations should
[578](https://docs.rs#578)    /// use `deserialize_in_place`.
[579](https://docs.rs#579)    ///
[580](https://docs.rs#580)    /// This method is stable and an official public API, but hidden from the
[581](https://docs.rs#581)    /// documentation because it is almost never what newbies are looking for.
[582](https://docs.rs#582)    /// Showing it in rustdoc would cause it to be featured more prominently
[583](https://docs.rs#583)    /// than it deserves.
[584](https://docs.rs#584)    #[doc(hidden)]
[585](https://docs.rs#585)    fn deserialize_in_place<D>(deserializer: D, place: &mut Self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<(), D::Error>
[586](https://docs.rs#586)    where
[587](https://docs.rs#587)        D: [Deserializer](https://docs.rs#945-1266)<'de>,
[588](https://docs.rs#588)    {
[589](https://docs.rs#589)        // Default implementation just delegates to `deserialize` impl.
[590](https://docs.rs#590)        *[place](https://docs.rs#585) = [tri!](https://docs.rs/lib.rs.html#111)(Deserialize::deserialize(deserializer));
[591](https://docs.rs#591)        [Ok](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Ok)(())
[592](https://docs.rs#592)    }
[593](https://docs.rs#593)}
[594](https://docs.rs#594)
[595](https://docs.rs#595)/// A data structure that can be deserialized without borrowing any data from
[596](https://docs.rs#596)/// the deserializer.
[597](https://docs.rs#597)///
[598](https://docs.rs#598)/// This is primarily useful for trait bounds on functions. For example a
[599](https://docs.rs#599)/// `from_str` function may be able to deserialize a data structure that borrows
[600](https://docs.rs#600)/// from the input string, but a `from_reader` function may only deserialize
[601](https://docs.rs#601)/// owned data.
[602](https://docs.rs#602)///
[603](https://docs.rs#603)/// ```edition2021
[604](https://docs.rs#604)/// # use serde::de::{Deserialize, DeserializeOwned};
[605](https://docs.rs#605)/// # use std::io::{Read, Result};
[606](https://docs.rs#606)/// #
[607](https://docs.rs#607)/// # trait Ignore {
[608](https://docs.rs#608)/// fn from_str<'a, T>(s: &'a str) -> Result<T>
[609](https://docs.rs#609)/// where
[610](https://docs.rs#610)///     T: Deserialize<'a>;
[611](https://docs.rs#611)///
[612](https://docs.rs#612)/// fn from_reader<R, T>(rdr: R) -> Result<T>
[613](https://docs.rs#613)/// where
[614](https://docs.rs#614)///     R: Read,
[615](https://docs.rs#615)///     T: DeserializeOwned;
[616](https://docs.rs#616)/// # }
[617](https://docs.rs#617)/// ```
[618](https://docs.rs#618)///
[619](https://docs.rs#619)/// # Lifetime
[620](https://docs.rs#620)///
[621](https://docs.rs#621)/// The relationship between `Deserialize` and `DeserializeOwned` in trait
[622](https://docs.rs#622)/// bounds is explained in more detail on the page [Understanding deserializer
[623](https://docs.rs#623)/// lifetimes].
[624](https://docs.rs#624)///
[625](https://docs.rs#625)/// [Understanding deserializer lifetimes]: https://serde.rs/lifetimes.html
[626](https://docs.rs#626)#[cfg_attr(
[627](https://docs.rs#627)    not(no_diagnostic_namespace),
[628](https://docs.rs#628)    diagnostic::on_unimplemented(
[629](https://docs.rs#629)        message = "the trait bound `{Self}: serde::de::DeserializeOwned` is not satisfied",
[630](https://docs.rs#630)    )
[631](https://docs.rs#631))]
[632](https://docs.rs#632)pub trait [DeserializeOwned](https://docs.rs/serde_core/de/trait.DeserializeOwned.html): for<'de> [Deserialize](https://docs.rs#554-593)<'de> {}
[633](https://docs.rs#633)impl<T> [DeserializeOwned](https://docs.rs#632) for T where T: for<'de> [Deserialize](https://docs.rs#554-593)<'de> {}
[634](https://docs.rs#634)
[635](https://docs.rs#635)/// `DeserializeSeed` is the stateful form of the `Deserialize` trait. If you
[636](https://docs.rs#636)/// ever find yourself looking for a way to pass data into a `Deserialize` impl,
[637](https://docs.rs#637)/// this trait is the way to do it.
[638](https://docs.rs#638)///
[639](https://docs.rs#639)/// As one example of stateful deserialization consider deserializing a JSON
[640](https://docs.rs#640)/// array into an existing buffer. Using the `Deserialize` trait we could
[641](https://docs.rs#641)/// deserialize a JSON array into a `Vec<T>` but it would be a freshly allocated
[642](https://docs.rs#642)/// `Vec<T>`; there is no way for `Deserialize` to reuse a previously allocated
[643](https://docs.rs#643)/// buffer. Using `DeserializeSeed` instead makes this possible as in the
[644](https://docs.rs#644)/// example code below.
[645](https://docs.rs#645)///
[646](https://docs.rs#646)/// The canonical API for stateless deserialization looks like this:
[647](https://docs.rs#647)///
[648](https://docs.rs#648)/// ```edition2021
[649](https://docs.rs#649)/// # use serde::Deserialize;
[650](https://docs.rs#650)/// #
[651](https://docs.rs#651)/// # enum Error {}
[652](https://docs.rs#652)/// #
[653](https://docs.rs#653)/// fn func<'de, T: Deserialize<'de>>() -> Result<T, Error>
[654](https://docs.rs#654)/// # {
[655](https://docs.rs#655)/// #     unimplemented!()
[656](https://docs.rs#656)/// # }
[657](https://docs.rs#657)/// ```
[658](https://docs.rs#658)///
[659](https://docs.rs#659)/// Adjusting an API like this to support stateful deserialization is a matter
[660](https://docs.rs#660)/// of accepting a seed as input:
[661](https://docs.rs#661)///
[662](https://docs.rs#662)/// ```edition2021
[663](https://docs.rs#663)/// # use serde::de::DeserializeSeed;
[664](https://docs.rs#664)/// #
[665](https://docs.rs#665)/// # enum Error {}
[666](https://docs.rs#666)/// #
[667](https://docs.rs#667)/// fn func_seed<'de, T: DeserializeSeed<'de>>(seed: T) -> Result<T::Value, Error>
[668](https://docs.rs#668)/// # {
[669](https://docs.rs#669)/// #     let _ = seed;
[670](https://docs.rs#670)/// #     unimplemented!()
[671](https://docs.rs#671)/// # }
[672](https://docs.rs#672)/// ```
[673](https://docs.rs#673)///
[674](https://docs.rs#674)/// In practice the majority of deserialization is stateless. An API expecting a
[675](https://docs.rs#675)/// seed can be appeased by passing `std::marker::PhantomData` as a seed in the
[676](https://docs.rs#676)/// case of stateless deserialization.
[677](https://docs.rs#677)///
[678](https://docs.rs#678)/// # Lifetime
[679](https://docs.rs#679)///
[680](https://docs.rs#680)/// The `'de` lifetime of this trait is the lifetime of data that may be
[681](https://docs.rs#681)/// borrowed by `Self::Value` when deserialized. See the page [Understanding
[682](https://docs.rs#682)/// deserializer lifetimes] for a more detailed explanation of these lifetimes.
[683](https://docs.rs#683)///
[684](https://docs.rs#684)/// [Understanding deserializer lifetimes]: https://serde.rs/lifetimes.html
[685](https://docs.rs#685)///
[686](https://docs.rs#686)/// # Example
[687](https://docs.rs#687)///
[688](https://docs.rs#688)/// Suppose we have JSON that looks like `[[1, 2], [3, 4, 5], [6]]` and we need
[689](https://docs.rs#689)/// to deserialize it into a flat representation like `vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]`.
[690](https://docs.rs#690)/// Allocating a brand new `Vec<T>` for each subarray would be slow. Instead we
[691](https://docs.rs#691)/// would like to allocate a single `Vec<T>` and then deserialize each subarray
[692](https://docs.rs#692)/// into it. This requires stateful deserialization using the `DeserializeSeed`
[693](https://docs.rs#693)/// trait.
[694](https://docs.rs#694)///
[695](https://docs.rs#695)/// ```edition2021
[696](https://docs.rs#696)/// use serde::de::{Deserialize, DeserializeSeed, Deserializer, SeqAccess, Visitor};
[697](https://docs.rs#697)/// use std::fmt;
[698](https://docs.rs#698)/// use std::marker::PhantomData;
[699](https://docs.rs#699)///
[700](https://docs.rs#700)/// // A DeserializeSeed implementation that uses stateful deserialization to
[701](https://docs.rs#701)/// // append array elements onto the end of an existing vector. The preexisting
[702](https://docs.rs#702)/// // state ("seed") in this case is the Vec<T>. The `deserialize` method of
[703](https://docs.rs#703)/// // `ExtendVec` will be traversing the inner arrays of the JSON input and
[704](https://docs.rs#704)/// // appending each integer into the existing Vec.
[705](https://docs.rs#705)/// struct ExtendVec<'a, T: 'a>(&'a mut Vec<T>);
[706](https://docs.rs#706)///
[707](https://docs.rs#707)/// impl<'de, 'a, T> DeserializeSeed<'de> for ExtendVec<'a, T>
[708](https://docs.rs#708)/// where
[709](https://docs.rs#709)///     T: Deserialize<'de>,
[710](https://docs.rs#710)/// {
[711](https://docs.rs#711)///     // The return type of the `deserialize` method. This implementation
[712](https://docs.rs#712)///     // appends onto an existing vector but does not create any new data
[713](https://docs.rs#713)///     // structure, so the return type is ().
[714](https://docs.rs#714)///     type Value = ();
[715](https://docs.rs#715)///
[716](https://docs.rs#716)///     fn deserialize<D>(self, deserializer: D) -> Result<Self::Value, D::Error>
[717](https://docs.rs#717)///     where
[718](https://docs.rs#718)///         D: Deserializer<'de>,
[719](https://docs.rs#719)///     {
[720](https://docs.rs#720)///         // Visitor implementation that will walk an inner array of the JSON
[721](https://docs.rs#721)///         // input.
[722](https://docs.rs#722)///         struct ExtendVecVisitor<'a, T: 'a>(&'a mut Vec<T>);
[723](https://docs.rs#723)///
[724](https://docs.rs#724)///         impl<'de, 'a, T> Visitor<'de> for ExtendVecVisitor<'a, T>
[725](https://docs.rs#725)///         where
[726](https://docs.rs#726)///             T: Deserialize<'de>,
[727](https://docs.rs#727)///         {
[728](https://docs.rs#728)///             type Value = ();
[729](https://docs.rs#729)///
[730](https://docs.rs#730)///             fn expecting(&self, formatter: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
[731](https://docs.rs#731)///                 write!(formatter, "an array of integers")
[732](https://docs.rs#732)///             }
[733](https://docs.rs#733)///
[734](https://docs.rs#734)///             fn visit_seq<A>(self, mut seq: A) -> Result<(), A::Error>
[735](https://docs.rs#735)///             where
[736](https://docs.rs#736)///                 A: SeqAccess<'de>,
[737](https://docs.rs#737)///             {
[738](https://docs.rs#738)///                 // Decrease the number of reallocations if there are many elements
[739](https://docs.rs#739)///                 if let Some(size_hint) = seq.size_hint() {
[740](https://docs.rs#740)///                     self.0.reserve(size_hint);
[741](https://docs.rs#741)///                 }
[742](https://docs.rs#742)///
[743](https://docs.rs#743)///                 // Visit each element in the inner array and push it onto
[744](https://docs.rs#744)///                 // the existing vector.
[745](https://docs.rs#745)///                 while let Some(elem) = seq.next_element()? {
[746](https://docs.rs#746)///                     self.0.push(elem);
[747](https://docs.rs#747)///                 }
[748](https://docs.rs#748)///                 Ok(())
[749](https://docs.rs#749)///             }
[750](https://docs.rs#750)///         }
[751](https://docs.rs#751)///
[752](https://docs.rs#752)///         deserializer.deserialize_seq(ExtendVecVisitor(self.0))
[753](https://docs.rs#753)///     }
[754](https://docs.rs#754)/// }
[755](https://docs.rs#755)///
[756](https://docs.rs#756)/// // Visitor implementation that will walk the outer array of the JSON input.
[757](https://docs.rs#757)/// struct FlattenedVecVisitor<T>(PhantomData<T>);
[758](https://docs.rs#758)///
[759](https://docs.rs#759)/// impl<'de, T> Visitor<'de> for FlattenedVecVisitor<T>
[760](https://docs.rs#760)/// where
[761](https://docs.rs#761)///     T: Deserialize<'de>,
[762](https://docs.rs#762)/// {
[763](https://docs.rs#763)///     // This Visitor constructs a single Vec<T> to hold the flattened
[764](https://docs.rs#764)///     // contents of the inner arrays.
[765](https://docs.rs#765)///     type Value = Vec<T>;
[766](https://docs.rs#766)///
[767](https://docs.rs#767)///     fn expecting(&self, formatter: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
[768](https://docs.rs#768)///         write!(formatter, "an array of arrays")
[769](https://docs.rs#769)///     }
[770](https://docs.rs#770)///
[771](https://docs.rs#771)///     fn visit_seq<A>(self, mut seq: A) -> Result<Vec<T>, A::Error>
[772](https://docs.rs#772)///     where
[773](https://docs.rs#773)///         A: SeqAccess<'de>,
[774](https://docs.rs#774)///     {
[775](https://docs.rs#775)///         // Create a single Vec to hold the flattened contents.
[776](https://docs.rs#776)///         let mut vec = Vec::new();
[777](https://docs.rs#777)///
[778](https://docs.rs#778)///         // Each iteration through this loop is one inner array.
[779](https://docs.rs#779)///         while let Some(()) = seq.next_element_seed(ExtendVec(&mut vec))? {
[780](https://docs.rs#780)///             // Nothing to do; inner array has been appended into `vec`.
[781](https://docs.rs#781)///         }
[782](https://docs.rs#782)///
[783](https://docs.rs#783)///         // Return the finished vec.
[784](https://docs.rs#784)///         Ok(vec)
[785](https://docs.rs#785)///     }
[786](https://docs.rs#786)/// }
[787](https://docs.rs#787)///
[788](https://docs.rs#788)/// # fn example<'de, D>(deserializer: D) -> Result<(), D::Error>
[789](https://docs.rs#789)/// # where
[790](https://docs.rs#790)/// #     D: Deserializer<'de>,
[791](https://docs.rs#791)/// # {
[792](https://docs.rs#792)/// let visitor = FlattenedVecVisitor(PhantomData);
[793](https://docs.rs#793)/// let flattened: Vec<u64> = deserializer.deserialize_seq(visitor)?;
[794](https://docs.rs#794)/// #     Ok(())
[795](https://docs.rs#795)/// # }
[796](https://docs.rs#796)/// ```
[797](https://docs.rs#797)#[cfg_attr(
[798](https://docs.rs#798)    not(no_diagnostic_namespace),
[799](https://docs.rs#799)    diagnostic::on_unimplemented(
[800](https://docs.rs#800)        message = "the trait bound `{Self}: serde::de::DeserializeSeed<'de>` is not satisfied",
[801](https://docs.rs#801)    )
[802](https://docs.rs#802))]
[803](https://docs.rs#803)pub trait [DeserializeSeed](https://docs.rs/serde_core/de/trait.DeserializeSeed.html)<'de>: [Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) {
[804](https://docs.rs#804)    /// The type produced by using this seed.
[805](https://docs.rs#805)    type Value;
[806](https://docs.rs#806)
[807](https://docs.rs#807)    /// Equivalent to the more common `Deserialize::deserialize` method, except
[808](https://docs.rs#808)    /// with some initial piece of data (the seed) passed in.
[809](https://docs.rs#809)    fn deserialize<D>(self, deserializer: D) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::Value, D::Error>
[810](https://docs.rs#810)    where
[811](https://docs.rs#811)        D: [Deserializer](https://docs.rs#945-1266)<'de>;
[812](https://docs.rs#812)}

[815](https://docs.rs#815)where
[816](https://docs.rs#816)    T: [Deserialize](https://docs.rs#554-593)<'de>,
[817](https://docs.rs#817){

[819](https://docs.rs#819)

[822](https://docs.rs#822)    where

[824](https://docs.rs#824)    {

[829](https://docs.rs#829)////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
[830](https://docs.rs#830)
[831](https://docs.rs#831)/// A **data format** that can deserialize any data structure supported by
[832](https://docs.rs#832)/// Serde.
[833](https://docs.rs#833)///
[834](https://docs.rs#834)/// The role of this trait is to define the deserialization half of the [Serde
[835](https://docs.rs#835)/// data model], which is a way to categorize every Rust data type into one of
[836](https://docs.rs#836)/// 29 possible types. Each method of the `Deserializer` trait corresponds to one
[837](https://docs.rs#837)/// of the types of the data model.
[838](https://docs.rs#838)///
[839](https://docs.rs#839)/// Implementations of `Deserialize` map themselves into this data model by
[840](https://docs.rs#840)/// passing to the `Deserializer` a `Visitor` implementation that can receive
[841](https://docs.rs#841)/// these various types.
[842](https://docs.rs#842)///
[843](https://docs.rs#843)/// The types that make up the Serde data model are:
[844](https://docs.rs#844)///
[845](https://docs.rs#845)///  - **14 primitive types**
[846](https://docs.rs#846)///    - bool
[847](https://docs.rs#847)///    - i8, i16, i32, i64, i128
[848](https://docs.rs#848)///    - u8, u16, u32, u64, u128
[849](https://docs.rs#849)///    - f32, f64
[850](https://docs.rs#850)///    - char
[851](https://docs.rs#851)///  - **string**
[852](https://docs.rs#852)///    - UTF-8 bytes with a length and no null terminator.
[853](https://docs.rs#853)///    - When serializing, all strings are handled equally. When deserializing,
[854](https://docs.rs#854)///      there are three flavors of strings: transient, owned, and borrowed.
[855](https://docs.rs#855)///  - **byte array** - \[u8\]
[856](https://docs.rs#856)///    - Similar to strings, during deserialization byte arrays can be
[857](https://docs.rs#857)///      transient, owned, or borrowed.
[858](https://docs.rs#858)///  - **option**
[859](https://docs.rs#859)///    - Either none or some value.
[860](https://docs.rs#860)///  - **unit**
[861](https://docs.rs#861)///    - The type of `()` in Rust. It represents an anonymous value containing
[862](https://docs.rs#862)///      no data.
[863](https://docs.rs#863)///  - **unit_struct**
[864](https://docs.rs#864)///    - For example `struct Unit` or `PhantomData<T>`. It represents a named
[865](https://docs.rs#865)///      value containing no data.
[866](https://docs.rs#866)///  - **unit_variant**
[867](https://docs.rs#867)///    - For example the `E::A` and `E::B` in `enum E { A, B }`.
[868](https://docs.rs#868)///  - **newtype_struct**
[869](https://docs.rs#869)///    - For example `struct Millimeters(u8)`.
[870](https://docs.rs#870)///  - **newtype_variant**
[871](https://docs.rs#871)///    - For example the `E::N` in `enum E { N(u8) }`.
[872](https://docs.rs#872)///  - **seq**
[873](https://docs.rs#873)///    - A variably sized heterogeneous sequence of values, for example `Vec<T>`
[874](https://docs.rs#874)///      or `HashSet<T>`. When serializing, the length may or may not be known
[875](https://docs.rs#875)///      before iterating through all the data. When deserializing, the length
[876](https://docs.rs#876)///      is determined by looking at the serialized data.
[877](https://docs.rs#877)///  - **tuple**
[878](https://docs.rs#878)///    - A statically sized heterogeneous sequence of values for which the
[879](https://docs.rs#879)///      length will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
[880](https://docs.rs#880)///      serialized data, for example `(u8,)` or `(String, u64, Vec<T>)` or
[881](https://docs.rs#881)///      `[u64; 10]`.
[882](https://docs.rs#882)///  - **tuple_struct**
[883](https://docs.rs#883)///    - A named tuple, for example `struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8)`.
[884](https://docs.rs#884)///  - **tuple_variant**
[885](https://docs.rs#885)///    - For example the `E::T` in `enum E { T(u8, u8) }`.
[886](https://docs.rs#886)///  - **map**
[887](https://docs.rs#887)///    - A heterogeneous key-value pairing, for example `BTreeMap<K, V>`.
[888](https://docs.rs#888)///  - **struct**
[889](https://docs.rs#889)///    - A heterogeneous key-value pairing in which the keys are strings and
[890](https://docs.rs#890)///      will be known at deserialization time without looking at the serialized
[891](https://docs.rs#891)///      data, for example `struct S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 }`.
[892](https://docs.rs#892)///  - **struct_variant**
[893](https://docs.rs#893)///    - For example the `E::S` in `enum E { S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 } }`.
[894](https://docs.rs#894)///
[895](https://docs.rs#895)/// The `Deserializer` trait supports two entry point styles which enables
[896](https://docs.rs#896)/// different kinds of deserialization.
[897](https://docs.rs#897)///
[898](https://docs.rs#898)/// 1. The `deserialize_any` method. Self-describing data formats like JSON are
[899](https://docs.rs#899)///    able to look at the serialized data and tell what it represents. For
[900](https://docs.rs#900)///    example the JSON deserializer may see an opening curly brace (`{`) and
[901](https://docs.rs#901)///    know that it is seeing a map. If the data format supports
[902](https://docs.rs#902)///    `Deserializer::deserialize_any`, it will drive the Visitor using whatever
[903](https://docs.rs#903)///    type it sees in the input. JSON uses this approach when deserializing
[904](https://docs.rs#904)///    `serde_json::Value` which is an enum that can represent any JSON
[905](https://docs.rs#905)///    document. Without knowing what is in a JSON document, we can deserialize
[906](https://docs.rs#906)///    it to `serde_json::Value` by going through
[907](https://docs.rs#907)///    `Deserializer::deserialize_any`.
[908](https://docs.rs#908)///
[909](https://docs.rs#909)/// 2. The various `deserialize_*` methods. Non-self-describing formats like
[910](https://docs.rs#910)///    Postcard need to be told what is in the input in order to deserialize it.
[911](https://docs.rs#911)///    The `deserialize_*` methods are hints to the deserializer for how to
[912](https://docs.rs#912)///    interpret the next piece of input. Non-self-describing formats are not
[913](https://docs.rs#913)///    able to deserialize something like `serde_json::Value` which relies on
[914](https://docs.rs#914)///    `Deserializer::deserialize_any`.
[915](https://docs.rs#915)///
[916](https://docs.rs#916)/// When implementing `Deserialize`, you should avoid relying on
[917](https://docs.rs#917)/// `Deserializer::deserialize_any` unless you need to be told by the
[918](https://docs.rs#918)/// Deserializer what type is in the input. Know that relying on
[919](https://docs.rs#919)/// `Deserializer::deserialize_any` means your data type will be able to
[920](https://docs.rs#920)/// deserialize from self-describing formats only, ruling out Postcard and many
[921](https://docs.rs#921)/// others.
[922](https://docs.rs#922)///
[923](https://docs.rs#923)/// [Serde data model]: https://serde.rs/data-model.html
[924](https://docs.rs#924)///
[925](https://docs.rs#925)/// # Lifetime
[926](https://docs.rs#926)///
[927](https://docs.rs#927)/// The `'de` lifetime of this trait is the lifetime of data that may be
[928](https://docs.rs#928)/// borrowed from the input when deserializing. See the page [Understanding
[929](https://docs.rs#929)/// deserializer lifetimes] for a more detailed explanation of these lifetimes.
[930](https://docs.rs#930)///
[931](https://docs.rs#931)/// [Understanding deserializer lifetimes]: https://serde.rs/lifetimes.html
[932](https://docs.rs#932)///
[933](https://docs.rs#933)/// # Example implementation
[934](https://docs.rs#934)///
[935](https://docs.rs#935)/// The [example data format] presented on the website contains example code for
[936](https://docs.rs#936)/// a basic JSON `Deserializer`.
[937](https://docs.rs#937)///
[938](https://docs.rs#938)/// [example data format]: https://serde.rs/data-format.html
[939](https://docs.rs#939)#[cfg_attr(
[940](https://docs.rs#940)    not(no_diagnostic_namespace),
[941](https://docs.rs#941)    diagnostic::on_unimplemented(
[942](https://docs.rs#942)        message = "the trait bound `{Self}: serde::de::Deserializer<'de>` is not satisfied",
[943](https://docs.rs#943)    )
[944](https://docs.rs#944))]
[945](https://docs.rs#945)pub trait [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/serde_core/trait.Deserializer.html)<'de>: [Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) {
[946](https://docs.rs#946)    /// The error type that can be returned if some error occurs during
[947](https://docs.rs#947)    /// deserialization.
[948](https://docs.rs#948)    type Error: [Error](https://docs.rs#304);
[949](https://docs.rs#949)
[950](https://docs.rs#950)    /// Require the `Deserializer` to figure out how to drive the visitor based
[951](https://docs.rs#951)    /// on what data type is in the input.
[952](https://docs.rs#952)    ///
[953](https://docs.rs#953)    /// When implementing `Deserialize`, you should avoid relying on
[954](https://docs.rs#954)    /// `Deserializer::deserialize_any` unless you need to be told by the
[955](https://docs.rs#955)    /// Deserializer what type is in the input. Know that relying on
[956](https://docs.rs#956)    /// `Deserializer::deserialize_any` means your data type will be able to
[957](https://docs.rs#957)    /// deserialize from self-describing formats only, ruling out Postcard and
[958](https://docs.rs#958)    /// many others.
[959](https://docs.rs#959)    fn deserialize_any<V>(self, visitor: V) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<V::Value, Self::Error>

[965](https://docs.rs#965)    where
[966](https://docs.rs#966)        V: [Visitor](https://docs.rs#1317-1720)<'de>;
[967](https://docs.rs#967)

[969](https://docs.rs#969)    fn deserialize_i8<V>(self, visitor: V) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<V::Value, Self::Error>
[970](https://docs.rs#970)    where
[971](https://docs.rs#971)        V: [Visitor](https://docs.rs#1317-1720)<'de>;
[972](https://docs.rs#972)
[973](https://docs.rs#973)    /// Hint that the `Deserialize` type is expecting an `i16` value.
[974](https://docs.rs#974)    fn deserialize_i16<V>(self, visitor: V) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<V::Value, Self::Error>
[975](https://docs.rs#975)    where
[976](https://docs.rs#976)        V: [Visitor](https://docs.rs#1317-1720)<'de>;
[977](https://docs.rs#977)
[978](https://docs.rs#978)    /// Hint that the `Deserialize` type is expecting an `i32` value.
[979](https://docs.rs#979)    fn deserialize_i32<V>(self, visitor: V) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<V::Value, Self::Error>
[980](https://docs.rs#980)    where
[981](https://docs.rs#981)        V: [Visitor](https://docs.rs#1317-1720)<'de>;
[982](https://docs.rs#982)
[983](https://docs.rs#983)    /// Hint that the `Deserialize` type is expecting an `i64` value.
[984](https://docs.rs#984)    fn deserialize_i64<V>(self, visitor: V) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<V::Value, Self::Error>
[985](https://docs.rs#985)    where
[986](https://docs.rs#986)        V: [Visitor](https://docs.rs#1317-1720)<'de>;
[987](https://docs.rs#987)
[988](https://docs.rs#988)    /// Hint that the `Deserialize` type is expecting an `i128` value.
[989](https://docs.rs#989)    ///
[990](https://docs.rs#990)    /// The default behavior unconditionally returns an error.
[991](https://docs.rs#991)    fn deserialize_i128<V>(self, visitor: V) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<V::Value, Self::Error>
[992](https://docs.rs#992)    where

[994](https://docs.rs#994)    {

[996](https://docs.rs#996)        [Err](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Err)(Error::[custom](https://docs.rs#304)("i128 is not supported"))
[997](https://docs.rs#997)    }

[1186](https://docs.rs#1186)    /// Determine whether `Deserialize` implementations should expect to
[1187](https://docs.rs#1187)    /// deserialize their human-readable form.
[1188](https://docs.rs#1188)    ///
[1189](https://docs.rs#1189)    /// Some types have a human-readable form that may be somewhat expensive to
[1190](https://docs.rs#1190)    /// construct, as well as a binary form that is compact and efficient.
[1191](https://docs.rs#1191)    /// Generally text-based formats like JSON and YAML will prefer to use the
[1192](https://docs.rs#1192)    /// human-readable one and binary formats like Postcard will prefer the
[1193](https://docs.rs#1193)    /// compact one.
[1194](https://docs.rs#1194)    ///
[1195](https://docs.rs#1195)    /// ```edition2021
[1196](https://docs.rs#1196)    /// # use std::ops::Add;
[1197](https://docs.rs#1197)    /// # use std::str::FromStr;
[1198](https://docs.rs#1198)    /// #
[1199](https://docs.rs#1199)    /// # struct Timestamp;
[1200](https://docs.rs#1200)    /// #
[1201](https://docs.rs#1201)    /// # impl Timestamp {
[1202](https://docs.rs#1202)    /// #     const EPOCH: Timestamp = Timestamp;
[1203](https://docs.rs#1203)    /// # }
[1204](https://docs.rs#1204)    /// #
[1205](https://docs.rs#1205)    /// # impl FromStr for Timestamp {
[1206](https://docs.rs#1206)    /// #     type Err = String;
[1207](https://docs.rs#1207)    /// #     fn from_str(_: &str) -> Result<Self, Self::Err> {
[1208](https://docs.rs#1208)    /// #         unimplemented!()
[1209](https://docs.rs#1209)    /// #     }
[1210](https://docs.rs#1210)    /// # }
[1211](https://docs.rs#1211)    /// #
[1212](https://docs.rs#1212)    /// # struct Duration;
[1213](https://docs.rs#1213)    /// #
[1214](https://docs.rs#1214)    /// # impl Duration {
[1215](https://docs.rs#1215)    /// #     fn seconds(_: u64) -> Self { unimplemented!() }
[1216](https://docs.rs#1216)    /// # }
[1217](https://docs.rs#1217)    /// #
[1218](https://docs.rs#1218)    /// # impl Add<Duration> for Timestamp {
[1219](https://docs.rs#1219)    /// #     type Output = Timestamp;
[1220](https://docs.rs#1220)    /// #     fn add(self, _: Duration) -> Self::Output {
[1221](https://docs.rs#1221)    /// #         unimplemented!()
[1222](https://docs.rs#1222)    /// #     }
[1223](https://docs.rs#1223)    /// # }
[1224](https://docs.rs#1224)    /// #
[1225](https://docs.rs#1225)    /// use serde::de::{self, Deserialize, Deserializer};
[1226](https://docs.rs#1226)    ///
[1227](https://docs.rs#1227)    /// impl<'de> Deserialize<'de> for Timestamp {
[1228](https://docs.rs#1228)    ///     fn deserialize<D>(deserializer: D) -> Result<Self, D::Error>
[1229](https://docs.rs#1229)    ///     where
[1230](https://docs.rs#1230)    ///         D: Deserializer<'de>,
[1231](https://docs.rs#1231)    ///     {
[1232](https://docs.rs#1232)    ///         if deserializer.is_human_readable() {
[1233](https://docs.rs#1233)    ///             // Deserialize from a human-readable string like "2015-05-15T17:01:00Z".
[1234](https://docs.rs#1234)    ///             let s = String::deserialize(deserializer)?;
[1235](https://docs.rs#1235)    ///             Timestamp::from_str(&s).map_err(de::Error::custom)
[1236](https://docs.rs#1236)    ///         } else {
[1237](https://docs.rs#1237)    ///             // Deserialize from a compact binary representation, seconds since
[1238](https://docs.rs#1238)    ///             // the Unix epoch.
[1239](https://docs.rs#1239)    ///             let n = u64::deserialize(deserializer)?;
[1240](https://docs.rs#1240)    ///             Ok(Timestamp::EPOCH + Duration::seconds(n))
[1241](https://docs.rs#1241)    ///         }
[1242](https://docs.rs#1242)    ///     }
[1243](https://docs.rs#1243)    /// }
[1244](https://docs.rs#1244)    /// ```
[1245](https://docs.rs#1245)    ///
[1246](https://docs.rs#1246)    /// The default implementation of this method returns `true`. Data formats
[1247](https://docs.rs#1247)    /// may override this to `false` to request a compact form for types that
[1248](https://docs.rs#1248)    /// support one. Note that modifying this method to change a format from
[1249](https://docs.rs#1249)    /// human-readable to compact or vice versa should be regarded as a breaking
[1250](https://docs.rs#1250)    /// change, as a value serialized in human-readable mode is not required to
[1251](https://docs.rs#1251)    /// deserialize from the same data in compact mode.
[1252](https://docs.rs#1252)    #[inline]
[1253](https://docs.rs#1253)    fn is_human_readable(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.bool.html) {
[1254](https://docs.rs#1254)        true
[1255](https://docs.rs#1255)    }
[1256](https://docs.rs#1256)
[1257](https://docs.rs#1257)    // Not public API.
[1258](https://docs.rs#1258)    #[cfg(all(not(no_serde_derive), any(feature = "std", feature = "alloc")))]
[1259](https://docs.rs#1259)    #[doc(hidden)]
[1260](https://docs.rs#1260)    fn __deserialize_content_v1<V>(self, visitor: V) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<V::Value, Self::Error>
[1261](https://docs.rs#1261)    where
[1262](https://docs.rs#1262)        V: [Visitor](https://docs.rs#1317-1720)<'de, Value = crate::private::[Content](https://docs.rs/private/content.rs.html#10-39)<'de>>,
[1263](https://docs.rs#1263)    {
[1264](https://docs.rs#1264)        [self](https://docs.rs#1260).[deserialize_any](https://docs.rs#959-961)([visitor](https://docs.rs#1260))
[1265](https://docs.rs#1265)    }
[1266](https://docs.rs#1266)}

[1268](https://docs.rs#1268)////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
[1269](https://docs.rs#1269)
[1270](https://docs.rs#1270)/// This trait represents a visitor that walks through a deserializer.
[1271](https://docs.rs#1271)///
[1272](https://docs.rs#1272)/// # Lifetime
[1273](https://docs.rs#1273)///
[1274](https://docs.rs#1274)/// The `'de` lifetime of this trait is the requirement for lifetime of data
[1275](https://docs.rs#1275)/// that may be borrowed by `Self::Value`. See the page [Understanding
[1276](https://docs.rs#1276)/// deserializer lifetimes] for a more detailed explanation of these lifetimes.
[1277](https://docs.rs#1277)///
[1278](https://docs.rs#1278)/// [Understanding deserializer lifetimes]: https://serde.rs/lifetimes.html
[1279](https://docs.rs#1279)///
[1280](https://docs.rs#1280)/// # Example
[1281](https://docs.rs#1281)///
[1282](https://docs.rs#1282)/// ```edition2021
[1283](https://docs.rs#1283)/// # use serde::de::{self, Unexpected, Visitor};

[1285](https://docs.rs#1285)/// #
[1286](https://docs.rs#1286)/// /// A visitor that deserializes a long string - a string containing at least
[1287](https://docs.rs#1287)/// /// some minimum number of bytes.
[1288](https://docs.rs#1288)/// struct LongString {
[1289](https://docs.rs#1289)///     min: usize,
[1290](https://docs.rs#1290)/// }
[1291](https://docs.rs#1291)///
[1292](https://docs.rs#1292)/// impl<'de> Visitor<'de> for LongString {
[1293](https://docs.rs#1293)///     type Value = String;
[1294](https://docs.rs#1294)///
[1295](https://docs.rs#1295)///     fn expecting(&self, formatter: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
[1296](https://docs.rs#1296)///         write!(formatter, "a string containing at least {} bytes", self.min)
[1297](https://docs.rs#1297)///     }
[1298](https://docs.rs#1298)///
[1299](https://docs.rs#1299)///     fn visit_str<E>(self, s: &str) -> Result<Self::Value, E>
[1300](https://docs.rs#1300)///     where
[1301](https://docs.rs#1301)///         E: de::Error,
[1302](https://docs.rs#1302)///     {
[1303](https://docs.rs#1303)///         if s.len() >= self.min {
[1304](https://docs.rs#1304)///             Ok(s.to_owned())
